blocks.text: What do 1:1:1, 1:2:2 and 1:5:5 mean?

The first number is the starter you keep. The second is the fresh flour you add. The third is the water. A kitchen scale makes the comparison repeatable. A spoonful of aerated starter and a spoonful of stirred starter can weigh different amounts.
At 1:5:5, you can use a smaller starting amount when you need a smaller build. Ten grams of starter plus 50 g each of flour and water gives you 110 g. The ratio stays the same.
Choose the ratio around your mixing time

Work backwards from when you can mix. Say you feed at 20:00 and need [ripe starter](/journal/when-is-sourdough-starter-ready) around 08:00. If your usual 1:1:1 feed peaks while you're asleep, first try 1:2:2 on a day when you can check the jar. If it still peaks earlier than you want, test 1:5:5 in the same spot with the same flour. A cooler room can also stretch the timing, so record the temperature if you change the location. Try one change at a time.

If your 1:1:1 feed is still climbing at 08:00, a larger feed is unlikely to solve a late peak. Consider an earlier feed or a consistently warmer spot within your usual method. If you have a newly created starter or one recovering from neglect, establish a reliable rise before building a bread schedule around it.

King Arthur compared 1:1:1, 1:2:2 and 1:4:4 under controlled conditions. The larger feeds took longer to reach their respective peaks in that trial. Use that as a reason to test the ratio, while relying on your own observations for the clock. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2025/03/13/sourdough-feeding-ratios)
Make enough for the recipe and the next feed
Add the recipe amount to what you want to keep. Then divide by the sum of the ratio parts.

Say you need 140 g of ripe starter and want 20 g left in the jar. At 1:2:2, you need five parts totalling 160 g. Each part is 32 g. Weigh 32 g starter, 64 g flour and 64 g water. If a few grams usually stick to your jar and spoon, build a little extra and record the actual amount you used.

If the recipe specifies a starter hydration, check that too. Equal added weights of flour and water give a 100% hydration feed. The finished jar is exactly 100% hydration only if the seed also contains equal weights of flour and water. For example, 30 g of 50%-hydration seed contains 20 g flour and 10 g water. Adding 30 g each of flour and water gives 50 g total flour and 40 g total water, or 80% hydration.
How to round a larger feed

For the same 160 g target at 1:5:5, one part is about 14.5 g. On a scale that reads whole grams, round the seed up to 15 g, then weigh 75 g each of flour and water. You get 165 g and keep the ratio intact. Weigh the recipe portion from the ripe build when it is ready and use the remainder for maintenance.

Keep the recipe build separate if you want your usual jar to stay small. Use a spoonful from the main jar as seed and keep the rest on its established [feeding routine](/journal/feed-sourdough-starter). This is also useful when your bake calls for a different flour blend. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)
Compare your ratios over two feeds

Use three identical straight-sided jars, all in the same spot. Stir the established starter before dividing it so each seed portion is as comparable as practical. Put 5 g in each jar, then add 5 g, 10 g or 25 g each of flour and water. Mark the starting level on each jar. If your scale struggles at 5 g, use 10 g seed and double each addition. Leave room for expansion.

Write down the feed time, temperature and flour. At each check, note the height and whether it is still rising, near its top or falling. If it was rising at 23:00 and falling at 07:00, the peak is somewhere in that window. Repeat the comparison on another day before relying on a single night's result. If a ratio reaches the right window but yields too much starter, scale the weights down together.

title: Sourdough Starter Feeding Ratios for When You Want to Bake
seoTitle: Sourdough Starter Feeding Ratios for Your Baking Schedule
description: Compare 1:1:1, 1:2:2 and 1:5:5 feeds by weight, build the amount you need, and find a peak window that fits when you want to mix dough.
intro: A sourdough starter feeding ratio tells you how many parts of ripe starter, flour and water to use, by weight. Start with 1:1:1 if you want a baseline for a healthy, established culture. Try 1:2:2 or 1:5:5 if your usual feed peaks too early and you need a later window. A larger feed often takes longer under comparable conditions. The useful timing is the one your jar shows with your flour and kitchen temperature. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2025/03/13/sourdough-feeding-ratios)

faqs.question: Which ratio should I use if I bake at the same time every week?
faqs.answer: Use the ratio that gives your established starter a repeatable window near mixing time in your kitchen. Build the right amount separately. Changing the total grams while keeping the ratio fixed solves a quantity problem. Changing the ratio is an experiment in timing. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2025/03/13/sourdough-feeding-ratios)

blocks.text: Get a clean jar and decide how much you need

Use a digital kitchen scale, a spoon or spatula and a clean straight-sided jar. Keep a band or piece of tape handy to mark the height. A clean jar with room for the starter to expand makes the next check easier. Use the flour and water you normally feed with, so a new ingredient does not change the conditions while you are learning the routine. [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

The 20 g example is a maintenance feed for an established culture. If your recipe needs 100 g, build more before you bake and allow for a portion to keep. If you are creating a starter from flour and water, follow the separate [first-week method](/journal/how-to-make-sourdough-starter).
Feed your starter in six steps

rows: 1. Set the baseline
Put the clean jar on the scale and press tare.
The display reads 0 g.
2. Keep the seed
Spoon in starter until the display reads 20 g. Set the excess aside.
20 g starter in the jar.
3. Add water
Tare again, pour in 20 g water and stir to loosen the starter.
20 g added water on the display.
4. Add flour
Tare again and add 20 g flour. Mix until there are no dry pockets.
20 g added flour on the display.
5. Mark the level
Scrape down the inside walls, settle the mixture and mark its height.
A clean starting line you can compare later.
6. Cover and label
Cover loosely and write down when you fed it.
A marked, dated jar with space to rise.

blocks.text: You can also weigh the ingredients without re-taring between additions. Start at zero with the jar on the scale. Stop at 20 g after adding starter, 40 g after adding water and 60 g after adding flour. Stick to one method per feed so the display is easy to interpret.

If you tip in a little too much water, record what went in. To keep an equal flour-and-water feed, match the flour to the actual water weight. If you kept 20 g starter but added 23 g each of flour and water, the build will be 66 g. Write down the changed weights if you want to compare how that feed behaves.
If the scale goes to sleep mid-feed

Write down each ingredient weight before you tare. If the display switches off, a note that says “20 g seed, 20 g water” tells you what is already in the jar. You can weigh the flour in a separate dish and add it without guessing. If you forgot whether the water went in, note the uncertainty and restart with known weights when a recipe needs a precise build.
Keep it out to bake or return it to the fridge

Baking soon. Leave the fed jar at a steady room temperature and check it as it approaches its usual high point. Look for expansion and bubbles throughout, and use the recipe’s cues for ripe starter. Take what the dough needs and retain some for your next feed.

Maintaining between bakes. Refrigerate an established starter according to your maintenance method. King Arthur’s fridge routine gives a refreshed starter a brief rest on the counter before returning it to the fridge and allows room-temperature feeds before the next bake. Follow the [fridge guide](/journal/sourdough-starter-in-fridge) for the full schedule. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)
What should I do with the excess?

The portion removed before adding fresh flour and water is commonly called discard. If it came from a healthy established starter, use it in a fully cooked recipe that calls for discard, or throw it away. If the starter shows signs of contamination, discard the entire culture. Keep raw starter and raw discard out of tasting spoons. [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [3](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)

A [feeding log](/journal/sourdough-starter-feeding-log) pays off when you can’t remember whether you kept 20 g or 40 g last time. [Crispy Crust](/) is being designed to remember the last weights for each jar and let you record the actual feed when it differs from the plan.

title: How to Feed Sourdough Starter by Weight
seoTitle: How to Feed Sourdough Starter by Weight
description: Feed an established starter with three 20 g weights. See when to tare, what to do with discard and whether to use the counter or fridge.
intro: To feed an established sourdough starter, retain 20 g of starter, then add 20 g of water and 20 g of flour. Stir, mark the level and cover the jar loosely. That gives you 60 g at a 1:1:1 ratio. Let it develop on the counter if you need ripe starter soon, or follow your fridge maintenance routine if you are putting it away. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)

faqs.question: What should I check after the feed?
faqs.answer: Read the current level against the mark you made when you mixed. Write down the time and whether the starter is climbing, near its high point or already falling. This gives you a usable comparison next time even if you never catch the exact peak.

blocks.text: Read the mark before you move the jar

Set a band around the freshly fed level. Scrape the walls above that line before leaving the jar to rise. Later, look across the surface at eye level and check the walls just above it. Photographing the mark and the jar from the same angle makes the next morning's comparison easier.

rows: Higher than the previous reading and still climbing
Rising
Check again before the time you normally mix.
At the highest reading so far, with little change between checks
Near peak
Look at the recipe's readiness cues before using it.
Below the last recorded height or a fresh residue line
Falling
Record the last higher reading and the first lower one.
Old streaks, no baseline and a single reading
Peak unknown
Clean the walls above the line and try a monitored feed.

blocks.text: A rounded surface can show the starter is still climbing. A flattening top can be useful alongside height, but flour and hydration can change how the surface looks. Compare the same jar across checks before drawing a conclusion from the shape of the top. [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2025/03/13/sourdough-feeding-ratios) [2](https://www.youkneadsourdough.co.uk/blogs/faq/how-to-manage-your-starter-when-it-peaks-too-soon)
Did it peak overnight?
Here are two illustrative cases.

A clean jar tells a story. You feed at 20:30, mark 2 cm and clear the glass above the line. At 23:00 the starter is 3 cm and still climbing. At 07:00 it is at 4 cm, with a fresh band around 5 cm. That supports a rise followed by a fall. Record “peak between 23:00 and 07:00” and log the two observations. Avoid picking an exact time inside that interval.

Old streaks leave the time unknown. You feed at 20:30 and notice a line at 5 cm the next morning. The glass was already streaked after stirring, and you made no evening check. Log “peak unknown”. Use a clean-walled jar on the next feed or start earlier on a day when you can look twice.

A fresh residue line can estimate how high the starter rose. It cannot give you the hour. If you only saw the starter at feeding and after it fell, the possible window is wide. An extra check before bed can make the window much more useful.
What if two checks show the same height?

Note the interval and check once more if you can. Two readings at the same level may capture a short plateau. They may also miss a small rise and fall in between. A clean glass wall and a photo at each check help you see the difference. For planning a bake, a useful label is “near peak at both checks” rather than a timestamp you cannot support.
If you compare photos, keep the jar on the same flat surface, with the band and the top of the mixture visible. A photo looking down into the jar can show bubbles but makes it harder to judge height.
How do I move the peak closer to mixing time?

Once you have a few readings, compare feeds with the same ratio, flour and room temperature. A larger feed can move the window later. A warmer spot can move it earlier. Change one condition, record the result and leave enough room in the schedule if today's kitchen is different. [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2025/03/13/sourdough-feeding-ratios)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned rise history is designed to keep that feed and its photos together. It would let you enter a peak window or leave it unknown, so your bake plan doesn’t depend on a time you never observed.
Can I use starter once it has started to fall?

If the starter has only just started to fall, consult the recipe’s instructions and compare it with your usual results. Some bakers use an active starter around peak, including shortly after it has begun to recede. A jar that has collapsed and been left for a long period is a less predictable starting point for a timed bake. Give it a fresh feed and use the recipe’s [ripeness cues](/journal/when-is-sourdough-starter-ready) if you need a reliable window. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/learn/guides/sourdough/faq) [2](https://www.youkneadsourdough.co.uk/blogs/faq/how-to-manage-your-starter-when-it-peaks-too-soon)

A peak describes this feed’s highest point. Before baking with a new starter, look for dependable activity across feeds and check that the culture meets the readiness criteria for your recipe. A single dramatic rise can be misleading during the first week. [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe) [5](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/12/19/why-is-my-sourdough-starter-not-rising)

title: When Is Sourdough Starter at Its Peak?
seoTitle: When Is Sourdough Starter at Its Peak?
description: Read the rise, high-water mark and fall in your starter jar. Learn how to log a peak window when the starter rises while you are asleep.
intro: Sourdough starter is at its peak when it reaches its highest level after a feed, before it falls. In a clear jar, the strongest clue is the change in height over successive checks. A fresh residue line above the current level can show that the starter rose higher while you were asleep. Record a window if you missed the top. Leave it unknown if the jar gives you too little evidence. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/learn/guides/sourdough/faq) [2](https://www.youkneadsourdough.co.uk/blogs/faq/how-to-manage-your-starter-when-it-peaks-too-soon)
targetQuery: when is sourdough starter at its peak

blocks.text: Question 1. Is it new or established?

A [new starter](/journal/how-to-make-sourdough-starter) has yet to rise reliably after comparable feeds. If it swelled on day two and barely moves later in the week, the first rise may have been an early burst. Continue the creation method you chose and watch the jar between feeds. A few surface bubbles and a brief rise are observations, while readiness requires a more repeatable pattern. [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe) [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/12/19/why-is-my-sourdough-starter-not-rising)

With an established starter, find the most recent feed that behaved normally. What changed since then? A chilly counter, a higher feeding ratio, a switch in flour or a long rest in the fridge are better leads than the bubbles alone. If the jar has spent a long time unfed, use the recovery guide for an established culture.
Question 2. Did you miss the rise?

Look for a clean high-water line above the current surface. A starter can look flat at breakfast even when it rose in the middle of the night. The residue is more useful if you scraped the walls above your starting mark after feeding. Old smears are harder to interpret. If the evidence is unclear, try a daytime feed so you can read the jar at two points before the next scheduled refresh.

Mark the starting height on a straight-sided jar. Note the level at the next check, even if it is unchanged. A change from 20 mm to 24 mm is a 20% rise in a straight-sided jar. That is easier to compare than writing “a bit bubbly” twice. With an irregular jar, compare photos or use a straight-sided container for the next feed.
Match the symptom to one experiment

headers: What to do at the next feed
rows: New starter rose once, then went quiet
Early activity before a stable pattern
Keep following the creation method and record successive feeds.
Jar looks flat and has a fresh line above the surface
A rise happened between checks
Feed earlier so you can watch the climb and fall.
Familiar flour and ratio, colder counter
The same feed may take longer
Compare the temperature with a normal feed before changing the ingredients.
Bubbles through a much looser mixture
A change in how gas is held
Weigh the feed and compare with your usual flour and hydration.
You switched to a much larger feed
A different rise window
Repeat the previous ratio with the same flour and location.
The starter spent weeks unfed in the fridge
The established culture may need several refreshments
Inspect first and use a documented recovery method if the jar passes that check.

blocks.text: A warmer spot can be worth testing if you found that the jar was colder than usual. Choose a steady room-temperature location and measure it. Avoid guessing from the thermostat across the room. If you warm the jar and change flour at the same time, you lose the comparison you need.
Two cases that can look identical at breakfast

Illustrative case A. On day four, a new starter shows scattered bubbles and hardly moves from the line. It rose dramatically on day two and has yet to repeat that rise. Keep the creation method steady. Record whether the next few feeds show progressively more activity, and check the temperature if the kitchen feels cool. The single early rise is too little evidence to schedule a loaf.

Illustrative case B. A mature culture fed at 20:00 looks flat at 07:00. There is a fresh band on clean glass above the surface. The next feed starts earlier on a day when the baker is home. Watching it rise and recede would help distinguish a missed peak from a sluggish culture. Once the baker has a usable baseline, they can test a later peak with a different ratio if their schedule needs one.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned feed history is designed to keep those comparisons in one place. A note such as “22°C, same flour, higher line before breakfast” gives you more to work with than a reminder that only tells you a feed happened.
Keep the next comparison small

Change one variable and name it in your notes before you feed. For example, “same flour and ratio, warmer spot” gives you a clear comparison. Record the next reading at about the same point after feeding. If the difference disappears on a repeat feed, you have a reason to keep observing before changing your routine again.
When to wait and when to change course

Give a new, uncontaminated starter time to establish a reliable pattern and follow the method you chose. For a mature culture, reassess if similar feeds at an appropriate room temperature keep showing little activity. Check your scale, flour, feed ratios and storage history before building a dough around it. If the starter remains unreliable, move the bake or use a known healthy culture. Discard any jar that develops [signs of contamination](/journal/sourdough-starter-mold). [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/12/19/why-is-my-sourdough-starter-not-rising) [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

title: Sourdough Starter Bubbling but Not Rising? What to Check Next
seoTitle: Sourdough Starter Bubbling but Not Rising? What to Check
description: Diagnose a bubbling but flat starter by age, the jar’s high-water mark, temperature and feeding changes. Test one variable at your next feed.
intro: If your sourdough starter is bubbling but not rising, first ask how old it is and whether it rose and fell between checks. A young starter can have a burst of activity followed by several quiet feeds. An established one may have peaked while you were away, cooled down, or changed how it holds gas after a flour or ratio change. If you see mould, suspicious pink or orange streaks, or unusual growth you cannot confidently identify, discard the culture and clean the jar. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/12/19/why-is-my-sourdough-starter-not-rising) [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/learn/guides/sourdough/faq)

blocks.text: Give the fridge jar one job

The fridge jar is the culture you keep between bakes. The build for the loaf is the portion you feed to get the right weight of ripe starter. They can come from the same culture without becoming the same job.

If you keep 50 g of seed and add 50 g each of water and flour, you have 150 g after mixing. That is the maintenance feed in King Arthur’s method. If you use a smaller established routine, keep the weights you already know work for your jar. Record the date, give the feed its short counter rest, cover loosely and store it in a consistently cold part of the fridge. A fridge door can experience more temperature changes than a shelf. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/05/16/how-to-store-sourdough-starter)
If you bake regularly on a weekend, the useful reminder is often when to take the jar out, especially if the culture needs more than one feed to recover.
An illustrative Thursday-to-Saturday routine
This example assumes a regularly maintained starter and a Saturday morning mix. Move the times when the jar or your recipe needs a different window.

rows: Thursday evening
Inspect the jar and refresh a measured portion on the counter. Mark the starting level.
You have a record of the feed and can compare its rise on Friday.
Friday morning
Check for expansion, bubbles through the starter and any higher line on the glass.
A familiar rise suggests the jar is getting back to its usual rhythm. Little activity calls for more observation and a further refresh under your method.
Friday evening
If the jar is reliably active, build what Saturday’s recipe needs plus a little to retain.
Choose the ratio from a feed you have watched, so you have a realistic morning check window.
Saturday morning
Check the build against the recipe’s cues. Weigh out the ripe amount for the dough.
Mix when the culture is ready. Shift the mix if the build is still slow.
After taking the recipe portion
Feed the portion you plan to keep and return it to its fridge routine after the counter rest.
Record the new date so you know when it is due for attention.

blocks.text: What if it barely rises on Friday?

Keep the recipe build off the critical path until the refresh responds. Check the temperature around the jar and look for a clean high-water mark in case you missed the peak. If the starter was healthy and responds more strongly across subsequent feeds, plan from the next reliable rise. If it still looks sluggish on Friday evening, aim for a later mix or another bake day. A deadline on the calendar does not tell you how the starter has recovered. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)
Keep the recipe build separate when the quantities differ

Say the loaf needs 100 g of ripe starter and you want 20 g left. At 1:2:2, a 120 g build uses 24 g starter and 48 g each of flour and water. If you lose a little to the jar and spoon, round up while preserving the ratio. Choose a build size that fits the loaf and keep your usual maintenance weights for the next week. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)
A weekly checklist you can keep on the fridge

items: Record the date of the last feed and the weights you used.
Choose the next maintenance day or the day you will take it out to bake.
Before mixing dough, check that the starter can repeat a familiar rise at room temperature.
Keep a reserve before weighing starter into the loaf.
Date the jar again when it goes back into the fridge.

blocks.text: If you skip a week of baking, continue the maintenance routine you follow. A jar with a long gap in its history needs a separate recovery check. If you find fuzzy growth, unusual [pink or orange](/journal/sourdough-starter-mold) streaks, or other suspicious changes, discard the starter and thoroughly clean the container. [3](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/learn/guides/sourdough/faq)

[Crispy Crust](/) is being designed with separate reminders for fridge maintenance and pre-bake refreshes. One can tell you the jar is due for care. The other can remind you to take it out early enough to check its rise before a planned mix.

title: How to Store Sourdough Starter in the Fridge Between Bakes
seoTitle: How to Store Sourdough Starter in the Fridge
description: Keep an established starter between bakes and plan a Thursday refresh, a Friday check and a Saturday mix, with a fallback if it rises slowly.
intro: Keep a healthy, established sourdough starter in a loosely covered jar in the fridge if you bake only occasionally. King Arthur’s maintenance method feeds the jar about once a week and gives it a short rest at room temperature before returning it to the fridge. Before baking, bring the starter back into its normal rhythm with enough room-temperature time and feeds to show a reliable rise. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/05/16/how-to-store-sourdough-starter)
targetQuery: how to store sourdough starter in fridge

blocks.text: Decide which route fits the jar

rows: Established jar, familiar appearance, clear history
Try a measured refresh and watch for renewed activity.
Flat surface liquid on a familiar, long-unfed jar
Check for separate signs of contamination. If the jar otherwise passes inspection, follow your usual refresh method.
Suspicious fuzz, streaks, growth or an unusual change you cannot identify
Discard the whole starter. Clean the jar and utensils thoroughly before restarting.
Young jar that never rose dependably
Return to the instructions for creating a new starter, provided there are no signs of contamination.
Unlabelled jar with an unknown history
If you cannot assess what it contains or how it was kept, start again with a known culture or a fresh flour-and-water method.

blocks.text: A long gap and an alcoholic smell can occur in a neglected mature jar. The overall history and appearance matter, and neither smell nor a photograph can establish that a starter is safe. Keep raw starter out of taste tests. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [3](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)
Use a refresh you can compare

items: Wash your hands and use a clean jar and utensil. If the starter passes your inspection, move a measured portion to the new jar.

Feed by weight using the familiar flour and a straightforward established-starter method. King Arthur’s equal-weight refresh uses 50 g each of retained starter, flour and water. Mark the height, record the time and cover loosely. [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)
Leave it at room temperature and check for bubbles and expansion. If the top is lower than a clear high-water mark, log that it may have peaked between checks.

Continue with the room-temperature refresh cadence in the method you are following. King Arthur’s pre-bake revival instructions use roughly 12-hour refreshments until the culture reliably rises again. Compare similar feeds and judge the response alongside your own recipe’s cues. [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)

blocks.text: Keeping the jar at a steady temperature and using the same ratio across the first comparisons helps you tell whether the culture is recovering. Record a change if you need to make one.
What improvement can look like
This is an illustrative log for an established jar, with example readings.

rows: First refresh
Bubbles appear and the level moves from 20 mm to 23 mm.
Record the movement. Allow more time before planning a mix.
Later comparable refresh
The level moves from 20 mm to 34 mm and bubbles are distributed through the jar.
Look for the response to repeat before relying on it.
Next comparable refresh
The jar follows its familiar rise again and meets the bread recipe’s readiness cues.
Build the quantity for the bake and leave enough to keep the culture going.

blocks.text: If progress stalls, ask whether the jar was cooler than usual or the rise happened while you were away. If a few consistent feeds produce very little response, reconsider the starter’s condition and whether replacing it is a better use of the time before your bake. If [suspicious growth](/journal/sourdough-starter-mold) appears at any point, stop and discard the culture. [5](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2021/09/02/did-i-kill-my-sourdough-starter) [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned recovery routine would let you log a return from the [fridge](/journal/sourdough-starter-in-fridge) separately from normal feeds. Having the last successful rise beside the new readings can help you decide when to schedule the bake.
What if you are not sure whether the first refresh worked?

Make the next check easier to compare. Clean the wall above the starting line, note when you fed it and photograph the level before you move the jar. A higher mark later can show that the feed rose while you were away. If the starter stays close to the baseline over several comparable feeds, a new culture from a known source may be more practical than postponing the bake again.

title: How to Revive a Neglected Sourdough Starter
seoTitle: How to Revive a Neglected Sourdough Starter
description: Know when to discard an old starter, how to refresh a familiar mature jar and what to record before relying on it to raise a loaf.
intro: You can try to revive an established sourdough starter that has been neglected if it shows no signs of contamination. Inspect it before stirring. Discard the whole culture if you find fuzzy growth, suspicious coloured growth, or unusual pink or orange streaks. If you cannot distinguish a suspicious change from normal separation, discard it and restart. A healthy-looking established jar can be given a measured room-temperature refresh. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/learn/guides/sourdough/faq)

faqs.question: When can I put the revived jar back into service?
faqs.answer: Use an established starter when it has returned to a predictable pattern across comparable feeds and satisfies the bread recipe’s readiness cues. Make the final build for the amount you need and keep a reserve. If you bake infrequently, date the jar when you return it to your fridge maintenance routine. [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)

blocks.text: What you need to start

items: A digital scale, a clean jar with room for expansion and a clean spoon or spatula.
Whole wheat or whole rye flour for the first mix, then unbleached all-purpose flour for later feeds. In the UK, look for comparable plain flour.
Drinking water, a loose-fitting lid, and tape or a band for the starting mark.
A spot at steady room temperature. The referenced method starts at about 21°C (70°F). [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe)

blocks.text: Wash your hands and start with clean utensils and a clean surface. Leave the lid loose enough for gas to escape. Flour is a raw ingredient and can carry germs. Keep the starter and anything you remove from the jar out of taste tests. Discard the early feed leftovers as you establish the starter. [3](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [4](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)
Day 1. Mix the first jar

Weigh 50 g whole wheat or whole rye flour and 50 g water into your jar. Stir until the flour is fully wet. Scrape down the walls, mark the level and cover the jar loosely. Leave it at room temperature for about 24 hours. Record the time and location so you can tell whether the conditions change.
Photograph the jar straight on, with the mark in frame. A straight-sided jar makes changes in height easier to compare.
Day 2. Keep 50 g and feed it

Keep 50 g of the mixture and discard the remainder. Add 50 g water and 50 g unbleached all-purpose flour. Stir and mark the new level. Leave it loosely covered for about another 24 hours. King Arthur’s method uses the same three weights for later feeds. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe)

You may see bubbles, little movement or a pronounced early rise. Record it and continue. A lively day two can be followed by a quiet spell. A single rise this early gives you little information about whether the culture will raise a loaf consistently. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/12/19/why-is-my-sourdough-starter-not-rising)
Day 3 onward. Observe between feeds

King Arthur’s method switches to approximately 12-hour feeds from day three. At each one, retain 50 g and add 50 g each of water and flour. Choose a pair of times you can repeat, such as 08:00 and 20:00. Mark the level as soon as you feed. Use a midday check or a clean high-water mark to learn what happens between feeds. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe)

rows: Bubbles but little movement
Activity is visible, with little measured expansion.
Keep the method steady and compare the next feed.
A dramatic rise followed by a quiet period
A young culture has shown a burst that has yet to repeat.
Record it and keep following the feeding schedule.
The starter rises reliably at similar temperatures
You have a pattern to check against your bread recipe.
Record how far and how quickly it rises on successive feeds.
Fuzz, suspicious growth or pink or orange streaks
There may be contamination.
Discard the entire jar contents and thoroughly clean the equipment.

blocks.text: For each diary entry, write the feed time, weights, temperature, starting height and next observation. Record a missed check and use the same photo angle when possible. Quiet days belong in the diary too.
What a useful day-five check looks like

If you feed at 08:00, a 14:00 reading gives you six hours of elapsed time. Record the height even if there is little change. If you only see the starter after it has fallen, note that you missed the top and check earlier after a similar feed.
When is it ready to bake?

In the referenced method, the target is a starter that roughly doubles within about six to eight hours after feeding and shows bubbles throughout. Look for that behaviour on repeated feeds before relying on it. Five days is a checkpoint in the recipe. A slower jar can need more time. Keep following the [feeding routine](/journal/feed-sourdough-starter) and check the temperature and weighing if the rise is still inconsistent. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/12/19/why-is-my-sourdough-starter-not-rising)

Consider an illustrative diary. The jar rises once on day two and stays close to its starting mark on days three and four. By day seven, its height is doubling after two comparable feeds, with bubbles throughout. The case for baking comes from those repeatable feeds. If day seven looks quiet, let the evidence change the bake date.

[Crispy Crust](/) is being designed to make a starter diary easier to keep. You could record the feed, temperature and photo at each check and see the quiet days alongside the later repeatable rises. That would help you decide whether to move the first bake without having to reconstruct the week from memory.
What if I need to troubleshoot?
The kitchen is cold. Measure the temperature beside the jar. Use the warm-room conditions in the method as your guide, and avoid sudden changes to several ingredients at once.

The starter suddenly stops rising. Check the walls for a missed peak, then compare the last two feeds. If you changed the flour or ratio, return to the routine you were following and record what happens. Use the starter troubleshooting guide for a fuller decision tree.

A clear layer has separated. In a [new starter](/journal/sourdough-starter-not-rising), this can be water separation. Consider what happened before it appeared and check for suspicious growth. Follow the creation method and use the separate surface-liquid guide if you need to tell the two situations apart. [5](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/is-the-clear-liquid-in-my-starter-hooch-or-water-separation/)

Once the jar rises dependably, build the amount your bread recipe calls for and keep a reserve. Continue with an established counter or fridge routine after the first loaf. [6](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/feeding-and-maintaining-your-sourdough-starter-recipe)

title: How to Make a Sourdough Starter From Scratch
seoTitle: How to Make a Sourdough Starter From Scratch
description: Make a sourdough starter from flour and water using a 50 g feeding method. Know what to record each day and how to judge when it can raise bread.
intro: To make a sourdough starter, mix flour and water, then keep a portion and feed it with fresh flour and water at regular intervals. A new jar can bubble early and go quiet again. Use a repeatable rise across feeds to judge when it is ready for bread. This guide follows King Arthur’s 50 g feeding method and gives you a way to record what you see each day. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/12/19/why-is-my-sourdough-starter-not-rising)
targetQuery: how to make a sourdough starter

blocks.text: Check the surface before you stir

Look at the top, the walls and the underside of the lid before moving the mixture around. Check whether a mark is on the wet starter itself or appears to be dried residue on the glass. The action to take depends on whether you can confidently identify an ordinary change. When an unusual patch remains doubtful, discard the culture.

rows: Fuzzy or hairy growth, including a pale patch
Discard all of the starter.
Unusual pink or orange streaks or spots
Discard all of the starter.
A surface film or patch you cannot identify
Discard it if contamination is suspected or you remain unsure.
Smooth liquid on a familiar mature starter after a long gap
It may be hooch. Inspect the whole jar for other changes before following your usual feed routine.

blocks.text: A clean-looking spot elsewhere in the jar offers little reassurance once you suspect mold. Throw away any portion already separated from that same culture. Keep raw starter away from tasting spoons. Raw flour can carry germs even when the jar looks ordinary. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [3](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)
What about hooch or dried starter on the rim?

[Hooch](/journal/sourdough-starter-hooch) can form as a layer of liquid on an established starter that has been left unfed. It can look grey or dark. That appearance is different from a patch with texture or raised fuzzy growth. If there are both liquid and suspicious signs, discard the starter. A photo, colour or smell alone cannot tell you that it is safe to keep. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/08/28/liquid-on-top-of-sourdough-starter)

A smear that has dried above the starter line can leave a pale crust on the wall. Clean walls make it easier to tell which marks are old. An unfamiliar film or new patch in an otherwise ordinary jar still calls for caution. If you are uncertain about a change, starting with a clean jar is the simplest way to resolve it.
Clean the jar and start over

Empty the starter into the waste. Wash and rinse the container and utensils thoroughly, then clean the work surface and wash your hands. Use fresh flour and water and clean equipment if you start another culture. You can also get a portion of a known healthy starter and put it into a clean jar. Use a loosely covered container with headroom for the next feed. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [3](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)

A dated feed and a clean starting line can help if the next jar changes unexpectedly. [Crispy Crust](/)’s planned starter history would let you keep a note of the last feed and consult reviewed guidance. The discard decision still belongs with what you know about the jar and what you see.
How can I make changes easier to spot next time?

Date the jar after feeding and wipe away fresh smears above the level. Use a clean spoon each time and follow a care routine that suits where you store it. If the jar is going into the [fridge](/journal/store-sourdough-discard), note when you plan to inspect and feed it again. These habits make the jar easier to read when you return. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [5](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/05/16/how-to-store-sourdough-starter)

title: Sourdough Starter Mold and When to Throw the Jar Contents Away
seoTitle: Sourdough Starter Mold and When to Throw It Away
description: Know when fuzzy growth, pink or orange streaks and uncertain patches mean you should discard the whole starter and clean the jar.
intro: If you see mold or suspect contamination in a sourdough starter, discard the whole starter. This includes fuzzy growth and unusual pink or orange streaks. Thoroughly clean and rinse the jar and utensils before restarting. Scraping off the visible patch leaves you with a culture you cannot assess at home. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/learn/guides/sourdough/faq)

faqs.question: Can I bake with the rest after removing the patch?
faqs.answer: Discard the entire starter if mold is present or contamination is suspected. Baking with the remaining part is an avoidable risk. Restart from clean equipment and use an established culture or the from-scratch method for a fresh jar. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

rows: Jar name and date

blocks.text: Put a band around the level immediately after feeding. Use a straight-sided jar if you measure height, and record the same units each time. If you move the jar to a new location, note the time and temperature there. Compare feeds only when the flour, ratio and temperature are similar enough for the question you are asking. Those conditions can change how the starter rises. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2025/03/13/sourdough-feeding-ratios)
Completed example for an overnight feed
These are illustrative entries.

rows: Fed 10 g starter, 20 g flour and 20 g water at 1:2:2. Kitchen measured 22°C (72°F). Started at 2 cm.
The level was 3 cm and climbing.
The level was 3.5 cm. A fresh line remained at about 4.5 cm.
Conclusion
The peak likely occurred between 23:00 and 07:00. The next feed will start earlier so the baker can observe more of the rise.

blocks.text: A window is useful for deciding when to look next time. If the glass was already streaked or the jar was stirred between checks, record “[peak](/journal/sourdough-starter-peak) unknown” and describe what you actually saw. You can still compare the next measured feed with this one.
Find a feed you can repeat

Start with a question such as “Can I feed after dinner and mix before work?” Find the feeds that used the same flour and ratio at similar temperatures. Compare their earliest and latest observations, then choose a time when you can look at the jar. For example, if you repeatedly missed the top between 23:00 and 07:00, a daytime feed on your next free day can help narrow the window.
How many feeds should I log?

Start with the next two or three feeds under similar conditions. That gives you a chance to see whether the timing repeats. Use a fresh sheet if you change the ratio, flour or location. Compare the changed feed with the earlier entries, then decide what to repeat.

intro: Use this sourdough starter feeding log to record what went into the jar, when you checked it and what it did. Print the sheet below and use one copy per feed. Its most useful entry is often a range for the peak. If you saw the starter rising before bed and falling in the morning, record the hours between those checks.
targetQuery: sourdough starter feeding log · printable variant also sampled

downloads.label: Starter feeding log — US Letter PDF

blocks.text: Keep, check or discard

rows: Established starter rose and fell after its last feed. A smooth liquid layer appeared during a long gap.
Inspect for signs of contamination. If everything else looks familiar, refresh it using your normal routine.
New jar shows a clear layer but has yet to rise dependably.
Record where the liquid sits and what happened beforehand. Water separation is possible. Follow the creation method if there are no signs of spoilage.
Jar has fuzzy growth, suspicious coloured streaks, an unidentified film or a change that makes you suspect contamination.
Discard all the starter, then thoroughly clean and rinse the jar.

blocks.text: Look before stirring. Once the liquid is mixed in, you lose one of the easier observations. A smooth layer can have more than one cause, and a photograph has no record of what happened between feeds. Keep raw starter out of taste tests. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [4](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)
Why does a mature starter get liquid on top?

An established starter can develop a liquid layer after sitting unfed. It may smell alcoholic and can darken in a refrigerated jar. Note how long it has been since the last feed and whether you saw a familiar rise and fall beforehand. A clear layer in a jar that has barely risen has a different history from a dark layer on a mature starter that has been in the [fridge](/journal/sourdough-starter-in-fridge) for a while. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/08/28/liquid-on-top-of-sourdough-starter) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/is-the-clear-liquid-in-my-starter-hooch-or-water-separation/)

Suppose you inspect a jar that rose after its last feed and was left in the fridge longer than planned. You find smooth grey liquid and no separate [signs of spoilage](/journal/sourdough-starter-mold). Hooch is plausible. Compare that with a new jar that has barely moved and shows a clear layer shortly after mixing. Keep the observation with that day’s feed rather than treating it as proof that the young starter needs an extra feed.
The three observations worth keeping

Write down the last feed time, the most recent rise you actually saw and where the liquid appeared. “Fed Sunday, rose and fell before refrigeration, smooth layer on Friday” gives you a clearer comparison than “liquid in jar”. If the starter has a suspicious patch, skip the logging experiment and discard the culture. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/is-the-clear-liquid-in-my-starter-hooch-or-water-separation/)
Should I pour off the hooch or stir it in?

For an otherwise normal established starter, Colorado State University Extension describes either option. Then feed the starter according to your usual method and watch for a familiar rise. Pouring off a liquid layer cannot salvage a jar with suspected contamination. If you see signs of spoilage or you remain unsure about an unusual patch, discard the whole starter. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

If the same change keeps appearing earlier than you expect, compare the dates, feed ratios and temperatures. Try one change to your routine and see whether it shifts the pattern. [Crispy Crust](/)’s planned starter history would let you record surface liquid beside those conditions. The useful bit is knowing what happened before it appeared.

title: Sourdough Starter Hooch and What to Do With It
seoTitle: Sourdough Starter Hooch and What to Do With It
description: Check whether liquid on your starter could be hooch or water separation, when to stir or pour it off, and when to discard the jar.
intro: A smooth liquid layer on a familiar, established sourdough starter can be hooch, a by-product of fermentation that may collect when a jar has been left unfed. In a new or weak starter, clear liquid can also be water separating out. Check the jar’s recent rise and feeding history. If you find mould, suspicious pink or orange streaks, or unusual growth you cannot identify, discard the whole culture. [1](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/08/28/liquid-on-top-of-sourdough-starter) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/is-the-clear-liquid-in-my-starter-hooch-or-water-separation/)

blocks.text: Give the maintenance jar and the bake jar separate jobs

The mother jar is the culture you keep from one bake to the next. The build is a portion of that culture fed to reach a particular weight and ripeness for one recipe. Keeping those jobs separate lets you make a large build without feeding a large jar every week. King Arthur and The Perfect Loaf both describe smaller maintenance routines for established starters. Follow a dedicated creation method if your culture is still getting established. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/a-smaller-sourdough-starter-recipe) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/keeping-a-smaller-sourdough-starter-to-reduce-waste/)

Start with quantities your scale can read reliably. In the example below, the mother jar uses 10 g of starter, 20 g of flour and 20 g of water. That is 50 g after feeding at [1:2:2](/journal/sourdough-starter-feeding-ratio). This is a worked quantity example. Choose a maintenance ratio and feeding interval that suit your own jar.

rows: Routine mother feed at 1:2:2
Build for a 150 g recipe portion
Build for a 60 g recipe portion

blocks.text: The build rows are alternatives. Each starts from a refreshed 50 g mother jar and leaves enough seed behind for another routine feed. A few grams can stick to a jar or spatula, so treat those totals as the amount mixed.
Work backwards from what the dough needs

For a recipe that needs 150 g, add a 20 g margin for jar losses or a little spare. At 1:2:2, divide the 170 g target by five total parts. One part is 34 g. Take 34 g from the active mother, add 68 g flour and 68 g water, and leave the build to ripen. From the approximately 16 g remaining in the mother jar, you can keep 10 g for its next feed.

For a small loaf needing 60 g, an 80 g build at the same ratio uses 16 g starter and 32 g each of flour and water. A build does not have to match the mother jar’s flour blend. If the recipe specifies a particular blend or hydration, use its build instructions and calculate the reserve separately. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/keeping-a-smaller-sourdough-starter-to-reduce-waste/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/what-is-a-levain-and-how-is-it-different-from-a-starter/)
Keep a small amount your scale can actually weigh

A display that rounds to whole grams has a larger effect on a 2 g scoop than on a 20 g scoop. Even a one-gram difference is half of a 2 g target. If the display jumps, fails to register a small addition or changes when you lift and replace the jar, use a larger batch with the same proportions. Doubling every number in a feed keeps the ratio unchanged.

Write down the three weights you actually used and the time of the feed. That lets you compare the rise with a similar feed next week. If you often bake twice a week, list both recipe quantities before you decide how large the mother jar needs to be. You can make two builds from the same jar if you still have enough seed for its next feed. A smaller batch still needs to be ready when you use it. Plan enough time for the build to meet the recipe’s cues.
Count discard over a normal week

Imagine you feed once in a non-baking week. Starting with 50 g of mother starter, keeping 10 g leaves 40 g to remove before the feed. With a larger 150 g routine where you keep 30 g, the equivalent amount is 120 g. Both examples use 1:2:2. The smaller routine produces 80 g less excess at that feed. Your weekly figure changes if you feed more often or use part of the jar for a bake. Use healthy established discard only in a suitable cooked recipe. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/a-smaller-sourdough-starter-recipe) [4](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned starter tools are designed to separate the maintenance feed from the recipe build. You could work out the grams for the loaf and keep a visible reserve for the mother jar before deciding how much to take.

title: How to Keep a Small Sourdough Starter and Still Have Enough to Bake
seoTitle: Low-Discard Sourdough Starter for Regular Baking
description: Keep a small sourdough starter between bakes, calculate builds for 60 g or 150 g of ripe starter, and track how much discard you produce.
intro: A low-discard sourdough starter can stay small between bakes. Keep a small mother jar on its regular feeding routine, then grow only the amount your next recipe needs in a separate build. Decide what you want left after mixing before you do the maths. That reserve is what keeps a big bake from using up your starter.

blocks.text: Read the recipe instruction before you feed

rows: “Add 100 g ripe starter”
Use an active portion at the required hydration and retain some culture for the next feed.
“Build the levain with starter, flour and water”
Mix those ingredients separately, then wait for the recipe’s ripeness cues before adding it to the dough.
“Refresh the starter, then use 120 g”
Check whether the refresh yields enough for the dough and a reserve. The recipe may be asking you to make the build in your usual jar.

blocks.text: Recipes sometimes use starter and levain for the same ingredient. Look for a separate set of weights and a waiting step. Those instructions tell you whether the recipe expects a build even when the heading just says “starter”.
Follow 120 g from jar to mixing bowl
Suppose you have 50 g of refreshed mother starter and the recipe calls for 120 g of ripe levain. The recipe’s build is 20 g starter, 50 g flour and 50 g water.

rows: Mother jar
Take 20 g for the build. Approximately 30 g stays in the mother jar.
Levain jar
Mix the 20 g seed with 50 g flour and 50 g water for 120 g before jar losses.
Mixing bowl
Add the ripe levain as directed. The mother jar remains available for the next feed.

blocks.text: If you regularly leave starter on a spoon or inside the jar, plan a few extra grams while preserving the recipe’s build proportions. A clean spatula helps when you need to scrape out most of the build. Use the recipe’s readiness signs rather than assuming the levain is ready as soon as it reaches 120 g.
When a separate build is worth it
Quantity. A [small mother](/journal/low-discard-sourdough-starter) jar may have only enough to seed a build. Growing a second jar for the bake lets you preserve the routine that has been working.

Flour. If your mother is fed white flour and the recipe calls for a whole-rye levain, feed the offshoot with the recipe’s flour. You can return to the usual white-flour feeds in the mother jar after the bake.

Timing. If you know how long the recipe’s build takes in your kitchen, you can feed it around the time you want to mix. Keep the mother on its usual schedule if the two feeds need different ratios. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/what-is-a-levain-and-how-is-it-different-from-a-starter/)

If the loaf needs a levain first thing in the morning, check when the recipe expects that build to be mixed. Write down the build time and the dough mixing time as two separate appointments. That leaves room to check ripeness before you commit the flour for the loaf.
Can I swap one for the other by weight?

Check flour blend, hydration and ripeness first. For example, a 100 g portion at 100% hydration contains 50 g each of flour and water. At 50% hydration, that same 100 g contains about 67 g flour and 33 g water. A straight swap would change what goes into the dough. If the recipe asks for a stiff build, follow its formula before experimenting with a substitution.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake timeline would place the mother feed and the levain build in separate steps. That makes it easier to see which jar needs checking and whether enough starter will remain after you mix.

If you’re unsure which to use, read the recipe from the mixing step backwards. Note the weight, the flour and water proportions, and what “ripe” looks like in that method. Then decide whether the jar on your counter already gives you what you need.

title: Levain vs Sourdough Starter and When to Build One
seoTitle: Levain vs Starter: What’s the Difference?
description: Learn when to use ripe starter directly, when to build a levain, and how to move 120 g of levain from jar to dough without using up your starter.
intro: A sourdough starter is the culture you maintain between bakes. A levain usually means a portion of that culture fed to make the right amount, flour blend and ripeness for one recipe. Both can raise dough. If your recipe asks for ripe starter directly and your jar matches its requirements, you may be able to use it as it is. If the recipe gives a separate levain formula, build that first. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/what-is-a-levain-and-how-is-it-different-from-a-starter/) [2](https://asbe.org/article/levain/)

blocks.text: Three reference points and what they assume

The rise percentages below are three reference points from Tom Cucuzza’s *The Secret of [Bulk Fermentation](/journal/when-is-bulk-fermentation-done)* guide. The guide uses a Tartine-style dough with 90% bread flour and 10% whole wheat in the flour blend, 75% water, 20% starter and 2% salt in its formula. It counts bulk from starter addition and assumes a shaped cold proof of 12–16 hours at about 3°C (37°F). The volume and height marks are calculated examples. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/The-The-SECRET-of-Bulk-Fermentation-Measuring-Dough-Temperature-and-Percentage-Rise.pdf)

headers: Target from a 40 mm start in a straight-sided tub
rows: 520 mL
52 mm
600 mL
60 mm
700 mL
70 mm

blocks.text: Use the temperatures as the source’s rounded equivalents. The rows describe dough temperature, measured at the dough. Room temperature and mixing-water temperature are useful context, but either can differ considerably from the dough itself. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature)
Why the warmer example uses a lower rise target

Fermentation carries on during shaping and while the dough cools in the fridge. The temperature at the centre takes time to approach fridge temperature. In this method, warmer dough is shaped at a lower [measured rise](/journal/measure-sourdough-rise-percentage) to allow for that carryover. This relationship belongs to the method and its proof conditions. A colder mix, warmer fridge, different starter proportion or room-temperature final proof changes the comparison. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/The-The-SECRET-of-Bulk-Fermentation-Measuring-Dough-Temperature-and-Percentage-Rise.pdf) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/the-mystery-of-percentage-rise-in-bulk-fermentation/) [4](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-final-proofing/)

The figures are shaping checkpoints for that formula, so keep the dough’s appearance and feel in the decision. If a recipe specifies a different endpoint, use its method and note what you actually observed. A loaf baked after a room-temperature final proof has a different timeline from one chilled overnight.
Put the mark on your tub
Record the starting volume at the point your recipe uses to begin tracking rise. In a straight-sided container you can also use a consistent starting height.
Target mark = starting reading × (1 + target rise ÷ 100).

For a 450 mL start and a 50% target, multiply 450 by 1.50. Put a mark at 675 mL. If you read 600 mL at a check, the increase is 150 mL on a 450 mL baseline, or about 33%. The number tells you how far the dough has expanded. Check temperature and the recipe’s other cues before deciding to shape.

Use marked volume if your tub flares towards the top. A height change in a widening container can represent a different volume change from the same height difference in a straight-sided one. If you start marking after the first fold, record that starting point. A late baseline can make a full-bulk reference hard to compare. [5](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)
Two illustrative bakes with the same formula

Imagine two batches of the reference dough, each marked at 400 mL. One is around 24°C (75°F) through the relevant checks and the other around 21°C (70°F). The warm example has a 600 mL reference mark and the cooler example has a 700 mL reference mark, assuming the same shaped cold proof. The readings are illustrative.

At 580 mL, both have risen 45%. The warmer batch is close to its reference mark, so you would check bubbles, aeration and handling against the recipe. The cooler batch has further to go by its reference. Give it time for another observation if it still feels tight. The different marks show why the same percentage can lead to two different next checks.
When to set the chart aside

Use the chart as context if you change the flour blend substantially, use a different amount of starter, move to room-temperature proofing, or miss the original starting measurement. Write down what changed. A second bake with the same formula and method helps you see which observations tend to predict the crumb you want. Review how the dough felt at shaping and how the cooled loaf looked, then change one thing in the next bake.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would keep dough temperature and rise next to the recipe stage and photos. That can help you compare two bakes with similar conditions and see why a reference chart worked for one loaf and needed a different interpretation for another.

Take the starting photo straight on with the band visible. At shaping, photograph the container from the same angle and write down both the mark you reached and how the dough handled. After baking, photograph a centre slice once the loaf has cooled. Those three checkpoints give you a comparison even if you decide to change the target on the next bake.

title: Sourdough Bulk Fermentation Chart by Dough Temperature
seoTitle: Sourdough Bulk Fermentation Chart by Dough Temperature
description: Read a sourdough bulk fermentation chart with its formula and cold-proof assumptions, then turn a target rise into a mark on your own container.
intro: A sourdough bulk fermentation chart gives you a reference rise for a particular dough temperature, formula and final proof. Start with your recipe’s cues. If you use a published chart, check its assumptions before transferring a percentage to your loaf. Once you choose a relevant target, convert it into a mark on your own container.

faqs.question: What should I put in the next bake record?
faqs.answer: Log the formula, starting reading, measured dough temperature, shaping time, fridge conditions and final loaf result. Write the chart reference separately from the rise you actually saw. Over several comparable bakes, that record gives you a better place to start than an isolated number.

downloads.label: Bulk fermentation chart — US Letter PDF

blocks.text: Set the baseline while you can still identify it

Choose a clean, clear container with straight sides and enough room for the sample to expand. Use a small portion big enough to measure with your ruler or the jar’s marks. Press it gently into the bottom to remove obvious voids, level the surface enough to read it and cover it loosely. Mark the top of the sample and note the time.

Follow your recipe if it starts bulk at starter addition. A sample taken after several folds measures the change from that later point. Write down that difference before you try to compare the jar with a chart that starts at mixing. If you consistently use the same later baseline, you can compare your own bakes that use it. [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)
Read the jar and the main dough together

items: Keep the sample beside the main dough, away from a heat source or draft that only reaches one of them.
At each check, read the level from the same angle. Measure the height from the bottom, using the same units as your starting height.
Record what the full batch is doing. Look for visible expansion, bubbles and how the dough feels in the container. Check its temperature at the centre if you can.
Use the recipe’s readiness cues when the two readings differ. A sample can be informative without behaving exactly like the dough you will shape.

blocks.text: If the sample starts at 20 mm and rises to 30 mm in a straight-sided jar, its [measured rise](/journal/measure-sourdough-rise-percentage) is (30 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100, or 50%. If the starting surface is uneven, record a range or level the starting sample more carefully next time. The sample height is an estimate of its volume change.
Why your sample can disagree with the full dough

A little jar changes temperature faster than a large batch. If you move warm dough into a cold kitchen, the small sample may cool first. If you put everything in a warmer area, the sample may warm first. The sample also sits undisturbed while you fold the main batch. Keeping the two together reduces one source of disagreement and gives you something useful to compare. [3](https://downloads.the-bread-code.io/the-sourdough-framework/book-hardcover.pdf) [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

rows: Start
20 mm at the chosen baseline
Baseline marked at mixing
Note the time and keep the vessels together.
Later check
30 mm, a 50% rise
Less expansion than you expect, still feels tight
Compare temperature and check the main dough again before shaping.
Next check
Sample has moved further
Full dough shows the recipe’s expected expansion and feel
Use the full dough’s signs and record the sample as a comparison.

blocks.text: These example readings show how to think through a disagreement. Use the sample’s movement and the full dough’s condition together. If the jar keeps leading your full batch, note the difference at several checks before you change your shaping decision. If your recipe uses a straight-sided main container and you can see the full batch clearly, its own measured rise may be the more direct observation.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would let you keep the aliquot reading beside the main [dough temperature](/journal/bulk-fermentation-chart) and a photo from the same check. That makes it easier to see whether the little jar tended to lead or lag across similar bakes.

title: How to Use an Aliquot Jar for Sourdough
seoTitle: How to Use an Aliquot Jar for Sourdough Bulk Fermentation
description: Take a useful dough sample, mark and measure its rise, and know what to check if the aliquot jar and main dough develop differently.
intro: An aliquot jar holds a small sample of dough so you can track its rise during bulk fermentation. Take the sample once your levain is evenly mixed into the dough, or at the starting point your recipe specifies. Place it in a straight-sided jar, mark the starting height and keep it near the main dough. Use its rise as one clue alongside the temperature and feel of the full batch. [1](https://flexsourdough.com/sourdough-bread-recipe/aliquot-method-sourdough/) [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

faqs.question: Do I need a dedicated aliquot jar?
faqs.answer: A clean, small, straight-sided container with a readable starting mark is enough. A specialist jar can make markings easier to read. The useful part is an early baseline, similar conditions and a second check on the main dough.

blocks.text: How to interpret what you see

rows: Floats
The spoonful held enough gas to stay on the surface.
Check how far the jar has risen and whether it has reached the recipe’s ripe stage.
Sinks
The sample did not stay afloat under those conditions.
Review the flour, hydration, handling and the actual rise in the jar.
Breaks apart or some pieces float
The sampling conditions made the result difficult to interpret.
Use the jar observations and skip another test unless you are comparing handling.

blocks.text: King Arthur’s demonstration found that a sample can float before the starter is ready. The Sourdough School also notes that active rye or whole-grain starters can sink. Taken together, those are good reasons to treat the result as a clue about one sample. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2019/01/02/the-float-test-for-yeast-dough-and-sourdough-starter) [2](https://www.sourdough.co.uk/what-if-my-sourdough-starter-goes-wrong/)
A simple side-by-side demonstration

On a feed that has reached its usual high point, note the time, flour, ratio and height against the starting mark. Lift a small, gently scooped sample into one glass of water. Take another portion of the same starter, stir it separately and put a similar-sized sample into a second glass. Use the same water temperature and look at both under the same conditions.

Record “floated”, “sank” or “broke apart” for each. If the results differ, the samples came from the same jar at the same time, so handling is a plausible explanation. This is a demonstration you can try. Record whichever result you actually see. Dispose of the samples after checking and keep raw starter out of taste tests. [4](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)
A more useful check before baking

Mark the level after feeding. See whether the starter [rises reliably](/journal/when-is-sourdough-starter-ready) across comparable feeds, whether bubbles are visible throughout, and whether it meets the ripeness cues in your recipe. Compare a rye starter with its own usual behaviour rather than using a white-flour jar as the baseline. A single early burst from a new culture is weaker evidence than a repeatable pattern. If the top has already fallen, note the high-water mark on the glass and check earlier after the next comparable feed. [5](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-starter-recipe) [2](https://www.sourdough.co.uk/what-if-my-sourdough-starter-goes-wrong/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned starter log would keep the feeding details and height observations together. That would make it easier to compare a doubtful float result with what the same jar did the last time it raised a loaf.

title: What the Sourdough Starter Float Test Can Tell You
seoTitle: Sourdough Starter Float Test: What If It Sinks?
description: Find out what the sourdough starter float test measures, why an active sample can sink, and what to check in the jar before baking.
intro: A sourdough starter can be ready to bake with even if a spoonful sinks. The float test shows whether that particular sample held enough gas to float. Flour, hydration and how you scoop it can change the result. Judge readiness from the jar’s repeatable rise and your recipe’s cues, especially if the starter contains rye or other whole-grain flour. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2019/01/02/the-float-test-for-yeast-dough-and-sourdough-starter) [2](https://www.sourdough.co.uk/what-if-my-sourdough-starter-goes-wrong/) [3](https://downloads.the-bread-code.io/the-sourdough-framework/book-hardcover.pdf)

faqs.question: Should I wait if my starter sank?
faqs.answer: Check the starter’s rise first. If it has barely moved and your recipe calls for an active, ripe starter, give it time and check again. If it follows its usual rise and meets the recipe’s cues, especially with a flour known to behave differently in the test, a sinking spoonful on its own gives you little reason to delay. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2019/01/02/the-float-test-for-yeast-dough-and-sourdough-starter) [2](https://www.sourdough.co.uk/what-if-my-sourdough-starter-goes-wrong/)

blocks.text: Two calculations you can use at the counter
Current rise (%) = ((current reading − starting reading) ÷ starting reading) × 100.
Target mark = starting reading × (1 + [target rise](/journal/bulk-fermentation-chart) ÷ 100).
The first calculation answers “How far has it risen?” The second answers “Where should I put the band?” For the second one, enter 50 for a 50% rise, so the multiplier is 1.50.

rows: 400 mL
Current reading is 600 mL
50% rise
20 mm in a straight-sided jar
Current reading is 32 mm
60% rise
320 mL
Target rise is 35%
432 mL target mark

blocks.text: A 50% rise leaves you with one and a half times the starting amount. Doubling is a 100% rise. A reading below the starting mark gives a negative result. Check whether the dough settled, fell, or was measured differently before drawing a conclusion.
Get a baseline that means something

Once the dough is mixed, follow the starting point used by your recipe and note when you marked it. Use a visible band or write down the volume in a marked tub. View it from the same angle each time. A domed surface can make the reading approximate. Choose a consistent way to read the level and note a range if the dough is uneven. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

If the first mark went on after a long rest or a fold, the percentage describes the change after that mark. You can still use it to compare bakes with the same baseline. If a chart starts from mixing, an after-fold measurement should be labelled as a different comparison. If the starting reading is zero or missing, put down the current observation and start a fresh record at the next suitable point. A percent change requires a positive baseline.
When height works and when to use volume

rows: Straight sides and a flat base
Use the height from the base or the marked volume.
Tapered walls with volume marks
Use the volume markings. The height changes at a different rate from the volume.
Rounded bowl with no markings
Move the dough to a suitable container at the recipe’s starting point, or use the recipe’s other observations.

blocks.text: Height is a useful stand-in for volume where the inside cross-section stays constant. An [aliquot jar](/journal/aliquot-jar-sourdough) has its own starting height. Keep the jar’s percentage separate from the reading for the full dough, especially when the two are at different temperatures. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [2](https://downloads.the-bread-code.io/the-sourdough-framework/book-hardcover.pdf)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would keep the starting mark, later readings and temperature against the same recipe stage. That would help you compare two bakes without having to remember whether you measured from mixing or after the folds.
