title: How to Measure Percentage Rise in Sourdough
seoTitle: How to Calculate Sourdough Percentage Rise
description: Calculate dough rise from two readings or find the exact mark for a target rise. Includes examples for jars and tubs and when height works.
intro: Subtract the starting reading from the current reading, divide by the starting reading and multiply by 100. Dough that goes from 400 mL to 600 mL has risen 50%. Use volume marks, or measure height in a straight-sided container with a flat base. Start both measurements from the same baseline and use the same units. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

faqs.question: Does the percentage tell me when to shape?
faqs.answer: Use the recipe’s target and check it alongside dough temperature, bubbles and how the dough feels. The calculation tells you the change since your mark. It helps you make the decision when the starting point, formula and proofing plan are comparable. [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/The-The-SECRET-of-Bulk-Fermentation-Measuring-Dough-Temperature-and-Percentage-Rise.pdf)

targetQuery: how to measure sourdough rise percentage

blocks.text: Know which of the three temperatures you are using

rows: Room temperature
Near the container, away from a local heat source
The conditions that can warm or cool your dough as it sits.
Mixing-water temperature
In the water just before adding it
One input you can adjust before your next mix.
Dough temperature
In the centre of the dough after mixing and at a later check
The conditions the dough itself is fermenting in.

blocks.text: These numbers can differ in one kitchen. In this illustrative record, the room is 20°C (68°F), the water is 28°C (82°F), and the finished mix is 24°C (75°F). An hour later the dough is 22°C (72°F). The warmer water helped set the starting temperature, while the dough cooled in its resting location. The two dough readings tell you more about what changed than either the room or water reading alone.
Where to put the thermometer

items: Clean the probe according to its instructions. Use an instant-read food thermometer with a tip you can place inside the dough.
Insert the tip far enough to read the middle of the mass. Aim away from the bowl wall or base. With a shallow dough, insert at an angle to keep the tip within it.
Hold the probe until the reading stabilises. Record the number with °C or °F, the time and the stage of the recipe.
If a reading seems out of place, take a second one near the centre from another angle. Note the difference if the batch appears uneven. Clean the probe after use.

blocks.text: If you use an aliquot jar, write the sample temperature and main [dough temperature](/journal/bulk-fermentation-chart) as separate entries when you can measure both reliably. A small sample can warm or cool more quickly. A useful record shows which mass each reading came from. [3](https://downloads.the-bread-code.io/the-sourdough-framework/book-hardcover.pdf)
What does “desired dough temperature” mean?

Desired dough temperature is the target for the dough at the end of mixing. A recipe’s target reflects its formula and expected process. For example, The Perfect Loaf’s beginner sourdough gives a target of 78°F (about 25–26°C). Other recipes use different temperatures and schedules. Use the target for the recipe you are baking and keep the actual reading beside it. [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature)

A cooler post-mix reading can mean a later check is needed, especially if the dough is expanding more slowly. A warmer reading is a reason to check earlier. Temperature helps explain the rate of change. The decision to end [bulk](/journal/when-is-bulk-fermentation-done) still depends on the recipe’s expansion and handling cues.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would let you record the post-mix reading and a later bulk reading beside the rise notes. That gives you something to compare if the same recipe behaves differently next week.

title: How to Measure Sourdough Dough Temperature
seoTitle: How to Measure Sourdough Dough Temperature
description: Learn where to take a sourdough dough temperature reading, what desired dough temperature means, and what to record if the batch cools.
intro: Measure sourdough dough temperature with a clean instant-read probe inserted into the centre of the dough after mixing. Wait for the reading to settle and keep the probe tip away from the bottom and sides of the container. Log this as your post-mix dough temperature. Take another reading during bulk if the dough moves to a different spot or develops more slowly than you expected. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2018/05/29/desired-dough-temperature)

faqs.question: What is the smallest useful temperature log?
faqs.answer: Write down the time, the stage and one dough reading. Add the room and water readings if you are trying to reproduce the mix or troubleshoot the temperature. Take a second dough reading when your schedule needs to change. Those two checkpoints can show whether the dough held its starting temperature or moved away from it.

blocks.text: Find the cold part of the process

Look at the starter before you mix. Was it reliably rising after comparable feeds, and did this build look ripe by the recipe’s standards? If it fell short of its usual pattern, fix that part first. If the starter behaved normally, take a reading in the centre of the dough after mixing and another during [bulk](/journal/when-is-bulk-fermentation-done). Compare those temperatures with the recipe and with any bake you have previously logged.

The kitchen thermostat is a starting clue. A metal bowl on a cold counter and a warm-water mix may each behave differently from what the room reading suggests. A temperature change after the mix can affect your schedule even when the ingredients and starter were the same. [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2018/05/29/desired-dough-temperature) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-bake-sourdough-bread-in-winter/)
Pick the change you can actually make

rows: You know tomorrow’s kitchen will be cool
Start earlier if your schedule allows, or adjust the mixing-water temperature according to the recipe.
Actual post-mix dough temperature and the first check time.
You are already in bulk and the dough is cooler than planned
Move the covered dough to a suitable, steadier warmer spot if one is available. Keep it away from direct heat and check the dough again.
Time moved, dough temperature and expansion at the next check.
The dough still needs time and you have to leave or go to bed
Move the bake or use a recipe-supported change for the stage you are in.
Stage, revised check window and the cue you are waiting for.
The starter never reached its usual activity before mixing
Give a future build time to ripen and compare similar feeds before relying on it.
Feed weights, temperature, time and rise.

blocks.text: A warmer environment changes the process gradually. Check the actual dough instead of assuming it has reached the temperature of its new spot. A cooler dough may simply need another observation. Give yourself a window you can actually check rather than committing to a shaping time from the clock alone. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-bake-sourdough-bread-in-winter/)
Set a check window before you start

If you already know when you have to leave the house, work backwards from the last time you can inspect the dough. Decide what you will do if it still needs more time at that check. For an unfamiliar recipe on a cold day, leave yourself room to shape later. Note the time of the next check when you move the dough, and keep the tub covered so you can compare the surface and the rise at that check.
Two illustrative paths from the same recipe

Imagine one recipe you have baked before. Your earlier loaf finished mixing at 24°C (75°F). On a winter bake, the dough finishes at 21°C (70°F). Keep the flour, starter amount and planned final proof the same for this comparison. The temperatures below are example readings. The decisions illustrate what you might do if the dough shows the stated cues.

Milder day. You take the first check as planned. The dough is holding near its starting temperature and is expanding as you remember. Keep the next planned check and look for the recipe’s shaping cues.

Colder day. At the same check, the dough has expanded less and still feels tight. You move it to a steadier spot, note the time and schedule another check. If its condition still points to more bulk, move the shaping time. If the later time conflicts with your evening, choose a later bake or follow a stage-specific alternative your recipe supports.

Use the bake result to make next week’s plan. Compare the conditions at shaping and the finished crumb. If you try warmer mixing water next time, keep the other changes small enough that you can see what effect it had.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake scheduler would keep your actual [dough temperature](/journal/sourdough-dough-temperature) and rise beside the tasks you still need to do. That would make it easier to see whether a later shaping check fits your day or whether to plan a different serving time.
[Read the worked sourdough schedule example](/tools/sourdough-schedule-calculator) with your recipe’s stage durations, then adjust the plan to what your dough shows.

title: How to Bake Sourdough in a Cold Kitchen
seoTitle: How to Bake Sourdough in a Cold Kitchen
description: See whether cool dough or a slow starter is delaying your sourdough. Choose a warmer resting spot, an earlier start or a later bake.
intro: If your sourdough is slow in a cold kitchen, check the dough temperature and the starter’s recent rise before changing the recipe. A ripe starter and a cool dough often call for more time, a suitable warmer resting spot or a later bake. If the starter itself is sluggish, give it time to reach the recipe’s readiness cues before mixing. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-bake-sourdough-bread-in-winter/)

faqs.question: Should I add more starter next time?
faqs.answer: Changing the starter amount changes the formula. If you want to test it, use a recipe that gives a cold-weather option or make one measured change and log the result. For a first comparison, a consistent starting temperature and a flexible check window are easier variables to interpret. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-bake-sourdough-bread-in-winter/)

blocks.text: Follow the dough through the stages
Mix → [bulk](/journal/when-is-bulk-fermentation-done) ferment → divide or preshape if needed → shape → final proof → bake.

In many sourdough recipes, bulk starts when the starter or levain is mixed into the dough and includes the folds. If your recipe counts from another point, write down that baseline. Bulk ends before you work the dough into its final shape. A recipe can include a preshape and bench rest in between, especially for multiple loaves. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

rows: Bulk fermentation
In a tub or bowl as one mass
Expansion since your starting mark, dough temperature, bubbles and how the dough feels.
Final proof at room temperature
Shaped in its basket, tin or other support
The recipe’s signs of expansion and aeration for a shaped loaf. Use a light poke if it suits the dough.
Final proof in the fridge
Shaped and covered for the recipe’s cold proof
The condition at shaping, time in the fridge and the recipe’s instructions for baking cold or allowing further proof.

blocks.text: Is a cold retard the same thing as final proof?

When a recipe chills the shaped loaf for its last rise, the cold retard is part of final proof. Some methods refrigerate the dough earlier, before shaping. That chill happens during bulk if the dough is still in its first rise. Check what stage the recipe says you are in before moving dough to the [fridge](/journal/refrigerate-sourdough-during-bulk). [4](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-final-proofing/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)
Why the cues change after shaping

During bulk you can mark a straight-sided tub and track rise from an early baseline. Once shaped, the loaf is in a basket or tin and has been handled, so that bulk measurement has done its job. Keep the expansion you saw and the time of shaping in your notes, then use the final-proof cues for the shaped dough.

A cold loaf can feel firm even if it has proofed enough. Check the recipe’s handling instructions and how the loaf looked before refrigeration. A longer chill also changes the dough’s temperature and rate of fermentation. It cannot be treated as a fixed amount of extra bulk. [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/) [4](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-final-proofing/)
An illustrative handoff

Say your recipe calls for shaping after the dough has reached its specified expansion and feels aerated. You make that decision at 19:00. After shaping, the instructions call for an overnight fridge proof. The bulk entry ends around shaping. Your next entry records the time the loaf went into the fridge, the fridge temperature if known, and the morning bake plan.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake timeline would give bulk and final proof their own checklists and times. When you review a loaf, you could see how long the dough spent in each stage and which observations led you to shape or bake.
If you are looking at one unshaped mass, check bulk cues. If you have a shaped loaf waiting for the oven, use the final-proof instructions for that loaf.

title: Bulk Fermentation vs Final Proof in Sourdough
seoTitle: Bulk Fermentation vs Final Proof in Sourdough
description: See when bulk fermentation ends, when final proof begins, and which signs to check before shaping, room-temperature proofing or chilling.
intro: Bulk fermentation is the first rise, while the dough is still in one mass. Final proof is the rise after the loaf is shaped, before it goes into the oven. The dough continues fermenting through both stages. Shaping changes what you are looking at and which cues you use. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

blocks.text: How to do a light poke

Lightly flour a clean fingertip if the surface is sticky. Press gently into the exposed dough, then lift your finger and watch what the dent does. Look at the response and the loaf together. Where the dough looks stretched tight or delicate, use a small press and avoid testing repeatedly in the same place. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/)

headers: What happens on shaped room-temperature dough
rows: The dent fills quickly
The dough may need longer. Check whether the loaf also looks tight and has expanded little.
The dent comes back gradually and remains slightly visible
Check the recipe’s other signs of readiness and prepare to bake if they agree.
The dent stays and the dough feels weak or fragile
Look for other signs it may have gone too far. Consider what happened during bulk and shaping before diagnosing it.
The dough is cold, very wet or difficult to handle
Give more weight to recipe cues and the recorded conditions.

blocks.text: Avoid timing spring-back with a universal number of seconds. Flour, hydration and dough temperature can change the response. Compare familiar doughs under similar conditions so the difference means something. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/)
Compare three checks from one formula

Use the same recipe and record the temperature each time. Compare a check soon after shaping with a later check at the recipe’s expected proof stage. If you have a third comparable loaf, use its later check to see how a more advanced proof feels. Note how the dough looks, whether it holds its shape and what you see in the finished crumb. A photo or short clip of the dent is easier to compare when the temperature and handling are written beside it.

This is a comparison protocol. Record what your own dough does. A quick rebound might fit a tight, early loaf at room temperature, while the same response in a chilled loaf can mean something different.
What to check if you are baking straight from the fridge

Look at how the dough developed before shaping, when it entered the fridge and the recipe’s stated cold-proof and bake method. If the recipe says to bake cold and the earlier cues matched, follow that method. If the dough was already behind at shaping or the fridge conditions changed, reconsider the schedule with those observations. The poke alone cannot recover that missing context. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-final-proofing/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would let you keep dough temperature, a proof observation and a photo together. That would make a later comparison more useful than trying to remember how quickly a dent sprang back.
Use the test as one clue during [final proof](/journal/bulk-fermentation-vs-proofing), and give it most weight when the dough is at room temperature and the other signs agree.

title: When the Sourdough Poke Test Is Useful
seoTitle: Sourdough Poke Test for Warm and Cold Dough
description: Use the poke test on shaped sourdough during final proof. Learn what quick rebound means and why chilled dough needs a different check.
intro: The poke test is most useful on shaped dough during a room-temperature final proof. A gentle press that comes back gradually and leaves a slight dent can be a useful clue that the loaf is close. Straight from the fridge, cold dough can feel firmer and spring back quickly even when the loaf has proofed enough. For a cold loaf, use the recipe’s cold-proof instructions and the dough’s history first. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2022/08/22/how-to-tell-if-bread-dough-has-risen-enough)

blocks.text: First make sure the loaf has cooled

Put the loaf on a rack and give the centre time to cool. A crust that feels cool to the touch can surround a warm interior. Use the recipe’s cooling guidance as a starting point and allow extra time for a large loaf. If you already cut one end, leave the rest on the rack and compare a fresh cut near the middle later. A warm cut can compress the crumb and leave sticky streaks on the knife. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

A cooled sourdough can feel moist and springy. If it tears into a tacky mass, compresses into a paste or leaves a persistent film on the blade, write down where that happens. Compare the centre and an off-centre slice. A single slice from the heel can miss the area that is causing trouble.
Use the location of the gummy crumb

headers: What you find in the cooled loaf
One change to try on the next bake
rows: Wet or pasty centre, with the crumb near the edges set
Review oven preheat, actual bake time, crust colour and the recipe’s signs of doneness.
Follow the recipe’s full preheat and bake sequence, then record the result at the centre. If you already did that, adjust only the bake time within the recipe’s guidance.
Tight, rubbery zones below or between a few large tunnels
Check whether the starter was ripe and whether the dough looked aerated and expanded at shaping.
If the starter was working normally and the dough was still tight at shaping, wait for the recipe’s bulk cues on a repeat bake.
Sticky or heavy across the slice after a flour or water change
Check the weights and the recipe’s flour and water guidance. Look for whether the dough felt unusually loose from the start.
Repeat with the original flour and recipe water, or reduce the added water by a measured amount if the recipe allows it.
Warm slice was sticky, later slice is set
Look at the time between taking the loaf out and slicing it.
Keep the bake the same and allow a complete cool.

blocks.text: These are starting points. A loaf can have both a short bake and a short bulk. Read the crust, the crumb and the notes together. If the bake log is blank, document the bake and cooling first. Those two details are straightforward to reproduce on a second loaf. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf) [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2020/11/05/how-to-produce-an-open-crumb-in-sourdough-bread)
What a centre-temperature reading can add

If the recipe gives an internal temperature, read near the centre and compare with the rest of its doneness guidance. For example, The Perfect Loaf’s beginner recipe gives about 208°F (97°C) for its loaf and also specifies an uncovered finishing phase and cooling on a rack. The reading helps you assess that bake. It cannot tell you how far the dough fermented or how the crumb will feel after cooling. [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

If you bake in a covered pot, note both the covered and uncovered times. “Baked for 45 minutes” is harder to reproduce than “lid came off at the 20-minute mark, and the loaf stayed in the oven until the recipe’s finish”. If the crust was already browning rapidly, also record where the pot sat in the oven. That observation gives you a place to start if the centre lagged again.
An example where the crumb gives two clues

Imagine a fully cooled loaf with a slightly gummy centre and two large tunnels over a tight base. The baker shortened the uncovered bake because the crust looked dark. Their notes also say the dough was still tight when shaped. Either clue could matter. First repeat the formula with a verified preheat, the recipe’s finishing guidance and the same cooling interval. If the centre sets but the tight base and tunnels remain, compare the [dense crumb](/journal/dense-sourdough-bread) patterns and review the starter and bulk on the next bake.

The planned [bake journal](/journal/sourdough-bake-journal-template) in [Crispy Crust](/) would let you keep a centre-slice photo beside oven times, cooling and the bulk notes. With those together, you can compare what changed between two loaves without relying on what you remember the next day.

title: Why Is My Sourdough Gummy After Cooling?
seoTitle: Why Is My Sourdough Gummy After Cooling?
description: Find out why sourdough stays gummy after cooling, what the location of the sticky crumb tells you, and what to change on your next bake.
intro: If your sourdough feels gummy after it has cooled completely, check where the crumb is sticky and how the loaf was baked. A tacky centre in an otherwise well-risen loaf calls for a look at the bake. Rubbery, tight areas around big tunnels also warrant a look at fermentation. If you cut the loaf while it was warm, let the remainder cool before you judge the texture. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done) [2](https://flexsourdough.com/sourdough-bread-recipe/gummy-sourdough/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf)

faqs.question: Can I fix a loaf that is already gummy?
faqs.answer: If the cooled bread is fully baked and just has a tacky texture, toast individual slices for serving. Treat a visibly raw, doughy centre as underbaked and keep it out of tasting. For the next loaf, write down what you changed and cut it in the same place after it cools. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done) [6](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)

blocks.text: Read the crumb against the kind of loaf you made

A whole-grain sandwich loaf and a white country loaf can both be well made and have different crumb. Start with a comparable bake or the recipe’s example. Notice whether the slice feels heavier than expected and whether the tight spots cover the whole slice or cluster around large voids.

rows: Uniform small cells and a heavy slice
Did the starter follow its usual rise after feeding? Was the flour blend or water different from the last bake?
If you changed flour, repeat with the recipe’s original flour. If the starter repeatedly fell short of its usual activity, check the feed routine before mixing another batch.
Tight base or thick dense bands around large tunnels
How much did the dough rise during bulk, and how did it feel when you shaped it? Was there a fold, seam or trapped dry flour where the gap appears?
If the dough was clearly tight at shaping and the starter performed normally, keep the formula and allow bulk to reach the recipe’s cues.
An even, compressed crumb after dough became weak
Did the dough lose strength during a long or unusually warm rise? How did it handle coming out of the basket?
Repeat the same formula and review the stage at which it lost strength. If the final proof was the one stage that ran long, adjust that stage first.

blocks.text: Several causes can leave similar marks. One cavity along a seam could come from shaping. Multiple tunnels with a dense base can also occur when the dough needed more fermentation. A photo makes those features easier to compare with the notes. [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-over-under-proofed/) [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/)
Check the starter, then the main dough

Starter. Look for a repeatable rise after feeds with the same flour, ratio and temperature. A jar that rose normally before mixing gives you a better starting point for investigating the dough. If the starter was barely active compared with its own history, keep the next recipe the same and establish a dependable feed before you test a longer [bulk](/journal/when-is-bulk-fermentation-done). [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2020/11/05/how-to-produce-an-open-crumb-in-sourdough-bread)

Bulk. Compare the actual dough temperature and rise with a bake you know. Look at the dough in the container and how it felt as you turned it out. A batch can develop more slowly than its predecessor despite the same time on the counter. Note whether the dough felt tight, light, or unusually weak at the point you chose to shape. [6](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [7](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature)

Shaping. If the dough looked expanded and aerated but the slice has a local cavity, note where the seam sat and how you folded the dough. Use the recipe’s shaping technique and keep bench flour away from surfaces you need to seal. A consistent shape lets you compare fermentation more fairly. [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/)
Choose one variable for the next loaf

Imagine the same flour, feed ratio and recipe produced two loaves. The second dough was cooler, reached a lower marked rise and felt tighter at shaping. Its slice had large holes and thick, dense areas. For the next loaf, keep the formula and shaping method. Measure the dough temperature again and judge bulk at a later check if it still feels tight. Write down the actual rise and handling cue that made you shape.

If the dough instead expanded normally but you changed to a much higher proportion of whole grain, compare another loaf with the original flour blend. Keep the timing checks and shape comparable. In both cases, changing one thing gives you a result you can learn from.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake comparison would put two centre-slice photos alongside their starter feeds, dough temperatures and shaping notes. It would help you spot which stage changed when the crumb looks similar for different reasons.

title: Why Is My Sourdough Bread So Dense?
seoTitle: Why Is My Sourdough Bread So Dense?
description: Compare an evenly tight crumb with dense patches around tunnels, then use the starter, bulk and shaping notes to choose your next change.
intro: A dense sourdough loaf can be tight all the way across, or it can have a few large holes surrounded by heavy crumb. Cut through the centre after cooling and identify which pattern you have. Then work back to the starter, bulk rise and shaping. The most useful clue is often the first stage that looked different from a loaf that worked. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2020/11/05/how-to-produce-an-open-crumb-in-sourdough-bread) [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf)

faqs.question: Does dense sourdough always need longer bulk?
faqs.answer: Check the evidence before adding time. If the dough was already slack and losing strength, a longer bulk could make the next loaf harder to handle. Use the underproofing and overproofing comparison to check what happened before the bake. If the dough was tight and barely expanded at shaping, more time may be the right first experiment. Compare the recipe’s expected cues and keep the final proof comparable while you test. [6](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-over-under-proofed/)

targetQuery: why is my sourdough bread dense

blocks.text: Compare observations before and after the oven

headers: Clues it may have been early
Clues it may have gone too far
rows: At the end of bulk
Little expansion for that recipe, limited aeration, tight feel.
Expanded earlier and now feels weak or hard to handle.
Shaped at room temperature
Loaf still feels tight and shows little expansion for its formula.
Loaf has lost strength or is difficult to move without deflating.
After baking and cooling
Dense areas with a few large irregular tunnels. Sometimes a tight base or a burst where the dough found a weak point.
Low profile and weak oven spring, especially if the loaf visibly lost shape before baking. The crumb may look compressed.

blocks.text: The table gives clues for a wheat sourdough that you can compare with its own recipe. Flour blend, hydration, shaping, and oven conditions also affect the result. A loaf shaped with loose tension can spread even when its fermentation is on track. If you use a [poke test](/journal/sourdough-poke-test), treat it as an observation during a suitable final proof. The response of cold dough can be misleading. [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf) [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/)
Separate bulk from final proof

When you compare two loaves, write down the moment you shaped each one. Before that point, record the dough temperature, rise from the same baseline, and whether the dough felt tight, aerated or weak. After shaping, record the proof location, time and condition. For a fridge proof, include the fridge reading if you have one and any time on the counter before chilling. [6](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

Suppose a loaf started final proof tight after limited expansion in [bulk](/journal/when-is-bulk-fermentation-done). A short final proof would add to the evidence of an early bake, but that record still cannot tell you which stage mattered most. Repeat the formula with the same final-proof conditions and first adjust the bulk decision. If the dough was well developed at shaping and became fragile only after a much longer proof than usual, compare a shorter final proof with bulk kept as similar as possible.
A published comparison and how to use it

Tom Cucuzza’s *A Tale of Four Loaves* compares multiple sourdough loaves with different fermentation histories. Use his photos and observations to see how changes in the dough and in the baked slice can line up. Compare your own loaf with the observation sequence as well as the appearance. A single matching tunnel or flat edge gives you a hypothesis to check. [7](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/video-transcript-underproofed-or-overproofed-a-tale-of-four-loaves/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf)

To make your own comparison, use one familiar formula and keep the flour, loaf size, shaping method, oven setup and cooling time consistent. If you want to examine final proof, keep bulk as similar as you can and vary the final proof only. If you want to examine bulk, hold the final-proof plan steady and record when each dough looked ready to shape. Slice through the same part of each cooled loaf. Photograph both slices in the same light and label the timings beside them.
What to do with an ambiguous loaf

Imagine a flat loaf with a tight base, a few holes near the top and no record of how it handled before baking. The crumb is compatible with insufficient fermentation, but the profile could also reflect poor shaping tension, a sticky turn-out or an oven issue. For the next bake, take a photo at the end of bulk and another immediately after you release the loaf from the basket. If it held shape until scoring but failed to spring in the oven, check preheat and baking setup. If it had already collapsed on release, look back at dough strength, proof and how it released.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would pair those photos with separate bulk and final-proof entries. You could review a loaf in order and see where its behaviour first changed, then copy the formula for a single-variable repeat.

title: Underproofed vs Overproofed Sourdough
seoTitle: Underproofed vs Overproofed Sourdough: How to Tell
description: Compare underproofed and overproofed sourdough before and after baking. See which signs to log and why a flat loaf can be ambiguous.
intro: To tell underproofed from overproofed sourdough, start with the dough’s condition before baking and use the cooled crumb to check your reading. An early loaf may look tight and show little expansion. A loaf that has gone too far can feel fragile, spread when released or lose the shape it held earlier. Both can bake into a flat loaf. When the photo is ambiguous, the temperature and observations from bulk and final proof give you a better next check. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-over-under-proofed/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf)

faqs.question: Can I fix underproofed or overproofed dough before baking?
faqs.answer: If shaped dough still looks tight and the recipe allows more time, check it again after a short interval. If it is fragile and deteriorating, extra proof time is unlikely to restore its strength. Bake promptly if you can handle it as the recipe directs. Record the point where it weakened so you can make an earlier decision next time. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/) [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/)

blocks.text: Start with the method your recipe was written for

Cold proof is the final rise of shaped dough in the [fridge](/journal/refrigerate-sourdough-during-bulk). In The Perfect Loaf’s published method, a wheat dough is mixed to a target of 78°F (about 25–26°C). It goes through folds and bulk, then gets shaped, covered and rested on the counter briefly before chilling. It is scored and baked cold. Use the recipe for its formula, bulk cues, oven setup and bake instructions. Its overnight time belongs to that sequence. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

Fermentation slows as dough cools. The middle of a loaf takes time to cool, even after the basket goes into the fridge. A dough that entered the fridge warm and well expanded can develop differently from a cooler or earlier dough on the same shelf. Measure the fridge where the loaf will sit if you are troubleshooting, and note the dough’s condition at shaping. [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)
Work backwards from the time the loaf goes into the oven

Say you want to load the loaf at 09:00. Subtract 16 hours and you get a fridge time of 17:00 the day before. This is a worked plan based on the published recipe. Your shaping and preheating windows have to fit around it.

rows: Before the 17:00 fridge target
End bulk when the recipe’s signs agree. Leave time for preshaping, the bench rest, shaping and the specified rest before chilling.
At 17:00, if the dough is ready
Cover the basket as the recipe directs and put it on the shelf you checked. Record the actual time and how the dough looked.
The next morning
Preheat on the recipe’s schedule. Leave the loaf covered and chilled until the oven and baking vessel are ready if the method calls for a cold bake.
Around 09:00
Score and bake as directed, then cool before slicing. Record when the loaf went in and how it handled on release.

blocks.text: The 09:00 time is when the loaf enters the oven. Add bake and cooling time if 09:00 is when people expect bread on the table. When you write a plan, put “oven” and “slice” on separate lines. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)
What to do if the evening runs later than planned

Suppose the dough is still tight when you expected to shape, and it enters the fridge at 19:00 instead of 17:00. If you bake at 09:00, you get 14 hours in the fridge. Moving the bake to 11:00 restores the planned 16 hours on paper. First check whether that revised time fits your day and whether the dough’s state and fridge conditions still match the method. Use this as scheduling arithmetic. A shifted clock cannot account for a change in dough development.

If you are already at the basket stage and the fridge is running warmer than usual, note the difference and use the recipe’s allowed range and cues rather than treating the original finish time as fixed. If the dough was still unshaped when you ran out of time, you are deciding whether to refrigerate during bulk. The overnight instructions for a shaped loaf apply after that step. [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake timeline would let you record when the basket actually went into the fridge and see how that shifts the morning bake and cooling windows. That is handy when shaping finishes later than the time you wrote down.

title: How Long to Cold Proof Sourdough Overnight
seoTitle: How Long to Cold Proof Sourdough Overnight
description: Plan an overnight sourdough cold proof around your recipe, fridge temperature and dough condition, with a worked morning bake schedule.
intro: For an overnight cold proof, use the fridge time specified for your shaped loaf. The Perfect Loaf’s beginner sourdough gives about 16 hours at 38°F (about 3°C), after bulk, shaping and a brief counter rest. That is a workable reference for that recipe. The time your loaf can spend in the fridge depends on how developed it was at shaping, how quickly it cools and how cold your fridge runs. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

faqs.question: Can I bake straight from the fridge?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your recipe uses a cold bake. The Perfect Loaf’s beginner method does. Get the oven and vessel ready first, then take the loaf out to score and load it. Other methods have the dough warm or continue proofing after it comes out. Use the instructions for the loaf you made. A firm feel or fast rebound from a poke on cold dough gives limited information about readiness. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/) [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/HOW-TO-USE-THE-DOUGH-POKE-TEST/)

targetQuery: how long to cold proof sourdough

blocks.text: Check the stage before you close the fridge door

headers: What refrigeration means for this loaf
rows: Mixed dough still in one mass
It stays in bulk. Follow your recipe’s cold-bulk instructions if it has them. If you are interrupting a warm bulk, record its condition and reassess on return.
End of bulk is close and you can shape now
Follow the recipe’s cues for shaping. If the recipe calls for a shaped cold proof, refrigerate the covered basket after the specified steps.
Already shaped in the basket
Use the recipe’s final-proof plan. The instructions for unshaped dough do not determine how long this loaf stays chilled.

blocks.text: If a dough has already expanded and is becoming weak, chilling can slow further change but cannot undo it. Note the condition you are starting from. A fridge rest also changes the timeline for a tight dough that still needs bulk, especially if it needs to warm after you return. [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)
Follow a cold-bulk recipe when you can plan ahead

King Arthur’s No-Knead Sourdough Bread uses three hours of room-temperature rise with folds before the unshaped dough goes into the fridge. It gives a chilled rest of at least eight hours and up to 48 hours for that formula. The next steps are preshape, a short bench rest, final shape and a room-temperature rise before baking. The recipe estimates about 2½ to 3 hours for that final rise. Those steps are part of the method and take time after the dough leaves the fridge. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe)

This recipe gives the fridge an explicit job and still leaves work to do on the other side. If your original formula only describes warm bulk and a [cold proof](/journal/cold-proof-sourdough-overnight) after shaping, the King Arthur timings do not transfer directly. You can use the published cold-bulk recipe for a future bake if it fits the way you need to split your time.
If you need to leave in the middle of bulk

items: Before chilling, cover the dough and note the time, dough temperature and rise from your original mark. Write down the last completed fold and whether the dough feels tight, aerated or weak.

On return, compare the rise with the same mark, check the dough’s temperature, and look at its surface and feel. Note what changed while it chilled. The cold dough may take time to warm and develop further.

If it is still short of the recipe’s bulk cues, continue bulk and set a new check. If the dough already meets the method’s conditions for shaping, plan the shaping and proof steps. Set the bake time once you know which branch you are in. [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

blocks.text: For example, say you chill a covered tub at 17:00, with the dough at 23°C (73°F), still tight and at 20% rise from its marked baseline. You return at 20:00 and it has expanded a little more, but the centre is colder and the dough still feels tight. Those readings describe an illustrative bake. Give yourself another bulk check. If you planned to serve at 23:00 and the recipe calls for a 45-minute bake and 90 minutes to cool, the loaf must be in the oven at 20:45. With bulk still in progress at 20:00 and [final proof](/journal/bulk-fermentation-vs-proofing) ahead, move serving to the next day. See the late bulk timeline for the next decision.

title: Can You Refrigerate Sourdough During Bulk Fermentation?
seoTitle: Can You Refrigerate Sourdough During Bulk Fermentation?
description: Learn when unshaped sourdough can go into the fridge, what to record before chilling and how to decide what comes next.
intro: Yes, unshaped sourdough can go into the fridge during bulk fermentation. A recipe designed for cold bulk gives you a clear plan for when it goes in and what happens after it comes out. If you are interrupting a room-temperature bulk, treat the fridge as a way to slow the dough down and plan a fresh assessment when you return. The dough can keep fermenting as it cools. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe) [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

faqs.question: Do I add the time in the fridge to my original bulk timer?
faqs.answer: Keep a record of elapsed time, but use the change in the dough to guide the next step. Write down when the dough went in, when it came out and how the rise and temperature moved. Those observations carry more information than a single timer that ran the whole time. [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

blocks.text: Work out which stage you are in

rows: Mixing
A rough, wet mass that has just come together.
Check the flour and water weights. Follow the recipe’s rest and mixing steps before deciding it needs more flour.
Early folds
Dough grabs your fingers but lifts as one piece and releases with lightly damp hands.
Use lightly damp hands for the folds and stop pulling once you meet resistance.
Late bulk
Dough was cohesive earlier and now smears, tears or loses its shape readily.
Check its rise and temperature. Review the recipe’s bulk cues before adding time or more handling.
Shaping
A tacky surface on a dough that still gathers and holds briefly.
Use a bench scraper and light flour where the recipe recommends it. Keep the surface you need to seal mostly clear of flour.

blocks.text: A wet dough can still strengthen with the recipe’s mixing and [folds](/journal/stretch-and-fold-sourdough). If you added too much water or changed flour, it may feel loose from the start. If the big change only showed up near the end, check the dough’s history before you change the formula. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2020/08/28/why-is-my-sourdough-so-sticky-plus-fixes-to-4-common-sourdough-mistakes-and-faqs/) [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2020/11/05/how-to-produce-an-open-crumb-in-sourdough-bread) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)
What to do when the dough sticks during shaping

Clear a small area and have a scraper ready. Turn out the dough as your recipe directs. With a cohesive wheat dough, use the scraper to release the part that clings to the counter and make a small move at a time. A light dusting on the exposed surface or your hands can help. Keep some grip on the work surface if your shaping method uses it to build tension. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

Pay attention to how the dough behaves once you stop. If it gathers and the surface tightens, continue gently and transfer it to its basket. If it tears or immediately flows back into a smear, repeated pulls can make it harder to handle. Use the support and handling that fit the recipe, and record the point at which it stopped holding together. Heavy bench flour can disguise the problem long enough to make it difficult to tell what happened.
Compare two doughs that both feel sticky

Imagine a dough at its first fold that clings to your fingers, then lifts cleanly once your hands are damp. It stretches in one piece and sits in a mound when you release it. That is a handling problem you can work around. Now imagine a dough that gathered neatly at earlier folds but feels looser and tears near shaping after an unexpectedly warm bulk. That change suggests checking the end of bulk against the recipe and an earlier successful bake.

Next time, change one thing. If the dough felt too wet from the first mix and stayed that way, weigh the ingredients again. Use the original flour if you switched, or try a measured reduction in recipe water where the method allows it. For example, 10 g less water with 500 g flour lowers the water-to-flour ratio by two percentage points, assuming the other ingredients and their contributions stay the same in that calculation. If the dough weakened late, keep the formula and record a temperature and rise reading before its usual shaping time. If it only flattens after you turn it out, use the shaping and basket release checks. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2020/08/28/why-is-my-sourdough-so-sticky-plus-fixes-to-4-common-sourdough-mistakes-and-faqs/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake notes would let you record whether the first handling problem showed up at mixing, folds or shaping, alongside flour, water and temperature. That makes it easier to choose a next-bake adjustment based on when the dough changed.

description: Find out why sourdough sticks at mixing, during folds or at shaping. Get a handling technique and a measured adjustment for your next loaf.
intro: Sourdough can feel sticky and still have enough strength to shape. Check when the stickiness appeared and whether the dough can hold together when lifted or folded. Tackiness from mixing often comes with a wet formula. Dough that was gaining strength and then starts smearing, tearing or flowing late in bulk needs a closer look at its temperature and fermentation. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2020/08/28/why-is-my-sourdough-so-sticky-plus-fixes-to-4-common-sourdough-mistakes-and-faqs/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

faqs.answer: Check the recipe and the stage first. Use a scraper, lightly damp hands during folds or a light dusting during shaping where appropriate. If your weights were right and the dough still holds together, those handling changes are a good first step. Adjust the formula on the next bake if the same problem starts at mixing again. blocks.text: Sunday at 11:00 means sliced bread on the table

Work backwards from the slice. In this example, a loaf out at 08:50 can cool for about two hours before 11:00. If your oven takes an hour to preheat, you need to be home and able to start it at 07:00. Choose your recipe before you put those times in the calendar. A bigger loaf, a longer bake or a slower oven moves the start earlier. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

This is an illustrative timetable adapted from The Perfect Loaf’s published beginner sourdough. It uses the recipe’s separate levain, flour-and-water rest, early folds and roughly 16-hour shaped cold proof. Its mixing and [fridge](/journal/sourdough-starter-in-fridge) assumptions matter. Use the recipe for the formula and the actual readiness cues. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)
Saturday mix and Sunday bake at a glance

headers: What can happen while you wait
rows: Saturday 06:00
Build the levain from ripe starter.
Let it ripen. Confirm the recipe’s expected readiness signs before mixing.
Saturday 10:15 and 11:15
Start the flour-and-water rest at 10:15. At 11:15, check the levain and mix the dough if ready.
The flour-and-water rest runs for about an hour. Note the dough temperature after mixing.
Saturday 11:45, 12:15 and 12:45
Do the three early fold sets. Cover between sets.
The dough rests between folds. Recheck the plan if mixing started late.
Saturday 13:00–14:30
Away from home.
Bulk continues after the last fold, provided the dough is behaving as expected.
Saturday around 15:15–16:10
Check bulk. Divide and preshape if ready, give the dough the recipe’s bench rest, shape and let it rest briefly before chilling.
Aim to have the baskets in the fridge around 16:10. Keep the actual time and dough notes.
Preheat as the recipe directs, aim to score and load the loaf around 08:00, and finish the bake around 08:50.
Keep the shaped dough chilled through preheat. The planned fridge time is just under 16 hours.
Put the loaf on a rack and slice at serving if fully cooled.
Allow roughly two hours for cooling.

blocks.text: If you bake two loaves and your oven only fits one covered pot, decide which loaf is for 11:00. The table reserves the oven for the first loaf. Plan the second loaf according to the recipe and the time you have later. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)
Check the outing before you commit

At 12:45, compare the dough with the same stage on a previous bake if you have one. If the first two folds happened on [schedule](/journal/sourdough-baking-schedule) and the last one is done, the remaining bulk rest is a plausible time to go out. A warm, rapidly expanding batch may need checking earlier. A levain that was late can push a fold into your outing. If either happens, move the outing, choose a later mix and serve later, or bake on a day with a wider window.
What if the dough is late after you get back?

Suppose bulk runs 90 minutes longer and the baskets go into the fridge around 17:40. Loading at 08:00 gives about 14 hours and 20 minutes of chilling. Loading around 09:40 keeps close to 16 hours, but a 50-minute bake followed by two hours of cooling puts slicing around 12:30. Choose the serving change if your dough and recipe still point to the longer proof. Write the new oven and slicing times down together. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

title: A Weekend Sourdough Baking Schedule for Sunday Bread
seoTitle: Weekend Sourdough Baking Schedule for Sunday Bread
description: Plan a Saturday sourdough mix and Sunday bake for 11:00 bread. See when to fold, go out, chill, preheat and let the loaf cool.
intro: To serve sourdough at 11:00 on Sunday, aim to load the loaf around 08:00 if your recipe bakes for about 50 minutes and allows up to two hours for cooling. Put the oven preheat before that, then plan Saturday’s work around the fridge time your recipe calls for. The schedule below leaves Saturday 13:00–14:30 free by putting the folds before the outing and the bulk check after it. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

faqs.question: Can I use this weekend plan with a different recipe?
faqs.answer: Use the same backwards planning. Replace the bake, cooling, folds and fridge windows with the ones that belong to your recipe. Then block the times you need to be home. The useful part of the timetable is knowing which waiting windows you can leave alone and which observations might change the plan.

blocks.text: A two-evening schedule with the workday free

This example uses King Arthur’s No-Knead Sourdough Bread. It calls for 227 g of ripe starter, three hours of room-temperature rise with folds, and a chilled rest of 8–48 hours for the unshaped dough. The next evening still needs time to shape, proof, bake and cool. The timings below are a planning example based on that recipe. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe)

rows: Day one before work
Arrange enough ripe starter for the evening, using a feeding routine that has reliably peaked around that time for you.
If the starter is rarely ready after that much time, do a trial feed or move the bake.
Day one 18:00
Mix if the starter is ripe. Cover the dough and start the recipe’s first rise.
You need to be home for mixing.
Fold at each check. Refrigerate the covered unshaped dough after the final fold.
Keep those three short windows clear.
Dough stays chilled.
No hands-on steps during work.
Take out the dough after about 21 hours of refrigeration. Preshape, give it the recipe’s 15-minute bench rest, then shape.
Start final proof once shaping is complete.
Day two around 20:00–21:30
Preheat about an hour before the anticipated bake. Look for the recipe’s expansion cue before scoring and loading.
With a final proof of around 2½–3 hours, an 18:30 shape puts loading around 21:00–21:30 if the dough is ready.
Day two around 22:00–22:30
Finish baking and move the loaf to a rack.
Allow it to cool completely. Plan to serve it the following morning if it is too late to slice.

blocks.text: Keep the chilled window tied to the recipe that specifies it. If your usual sourdough calls for a shaped loaf in the [fridge](/journal/refrigerate-sourdough-during-bulk), the hands-on tasks after work will be different. Write down what goes into the fridge and what still has to happen when it comes out. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)
A plan that does not fit the same workday

Suppose you mix at 07:00 and have to leave at 07:30. The King Arthur example would put its first fold at 08:00 and its later folds at 09:00 and 10:00. All three land while you are away. Leaving the dough out through the entire workday changes that method. Mixing at 18:00 moves those tasks into the hours you are available. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe)

Now suppose you are also out on the second evening. Moving the 18:00 shape to 18:00 on day three would give 45 hours in the fridge if it went in at 21:00 on day one. That is within the published range for this formula, with three hours left before its stated upper end. If you cannot commit to that window, start the bake on another day. A plan that looks clear at mixing can still fail if the shaping appointment is missing.
Build the workweek plan around your real constraints

Write down the time you can mix and the latest time you are willing to stay up for the oven. Add the steps that need you to be present. Then fill in the stretches when the dough can rest. Use a range for final proof and baking rather than planning a guaranteed end to the minute.

title: A Sourdough Baking Schedule for a Full Workday
seoTitle: Sourdough Baking Schedule for Working People
description: Fit sourdough around a full workday with two evening windows, a recipe-supported fridge rest and a clear example of a schedule that fails.
intro: You can bake sourdough around a 9-to-5 if your recipe’s hands-on steps fit the hours you are home. If you are free before 07:30 and after 18:00, a recipe with a planned unshaped fridge rest can span the workday. One option is to mix and fold after work on day one, refrigerate the dough while you work on day two, then shape, proof and bake that evening. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe)

faqs.question: Can I bake on the evening I get home?
faqs.answer: Yes if you have a recipe and dough already at the right stage, plus time for the remaining proof, bake and cooling. In this worked plan, baking may finish around 22:00 or later. If you want bread for dinner, bake the day before or choose a tested schedule that puts the loaf in the oven earlier. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/no-knead-sourdough-bread-recipe)

blocks.text: Check the dough and the time you have left

rows: Unshaped, cool and still tight
Check the marked rise and actual dough temperature. Give it more time if the recipe’s cues are still missing. Set a time when you can check again.
Unshaped and ready to divide or shape
If you can complete the remaining hands-on steps, shape and follow your recipe’s final-proof plan.
Unshaped and you have to stop before it is ready
If a fridge interruption fits the method and the dough’s condition, cover and refrigerate it. Record where it was in bulk and reassess when you return.
Unshaped, already fragile and losing strength
Check whether the dough has gone further than planned. More time may make handling harder. Use the recipe’s next workable step while the dough still holds together.
Already shaped
Check the recipe’s proof method and plan the oven and cooling. An unshaped-bulk rescue does not apply at this stage.

blocks.text: If the starter was slow before mixing, note it when you review the bake. Once the starter is already in the dough, the observations you can act on are the dough’s progress and the time you can give it. A warm spot may help a cool batch develop, but check the dough again after moving it. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature) [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-bake-sourdough-bread-in-winter/)
A 21:00 check when you planned to shape at 20:00

Imagine a dough mixed at 16:00. At 21:00, it is at 21°C (70°F), 25% above its starting mark and still tight. At shaping on your last good bake of the same formula, it felt aerated and showed more expansion. The example readings describe this batch. They do not set the right rise for another formula.

If you can stay up, [schedule](/journal/sourdough-baking-schedule) a 21:30 check. If the dough then meets the recipe’s bulk cues, shape it and use the recipe’s final-proof instructions. If it is still behind and you have to stop, use the recipe’s supported interruption or the mid-bulk refrigeration guidance. Log the [fridge](/journal/refrigerate-sourdough-during-bulk) time, temperature and rise, then make the next decision when you see the dough in the morning. A cold tub can still expand while cooling. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)
Move the serving time if it no longer fits

Suppose the dough needs to finish bulk the following morning and your original plan was to serve at 08:00. You still have to shape, proof, preheat, bake and cool. With a 50-minute bake and two hours of cooling in the recipe, a loaf served at 08:00 would have to enter the oven around 05:10, with the earlier stages already complete. Move breakfast to a later serving slot or use another loaf. [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [6](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

When you revise the plan, keep the original mix, folds and earlier readings in your notes. Cross out the future times you can no longer make. Then write down the next check and the first likely time you can be at the oven. This separates the hours that have already passed from the steps the dough still needs.

title: What to Do When Sourdough Bulk Fermentation Is Taking Too Long
seoTitle: Sourdough Bulk Fermentation Taking Too Long?
description: Check dough temperature, rise and feel when bulk runs late. See what to do at bedtime and when to move the bake or serving time.
intro: If sourdough bulk fermentation is taking too long, check dough temperature, rise and feel before you change the schedule. If the dough is still tight and short of the recipe’s cues, set another check while you are available. If you have to stop for the night, assess whether a supported fridge interruption fits your dough and your recipe. If the dough is already shaped, you are planning final proof. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

faqs.question: Can I leave bulk fermentation out until morning?
faqs.answer: Only use an overnight room-temperature bulk when the recipe and conditions support it. A dough that was meant to finish that evening can go too far while you sleep. If you need to stop, check the method for a chilled interruption and reassess the unshaped dough in the morning. [1](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

targetQuery: sourdough bulk fermentation taking too long

blocks.text: Look for the first change in shape

rows: During the rest after preshaping
The round relaxes a little and stays rounded, or quickly flows into a flat mass.
A little relaxation can help final shaping. If it flows, check how it held together through the last fold and at the end of bulk.
Immediately after final shaping
The skin never tightens, the seam opens, or the dough tears with another pull.
Check whether the shaping method had enough grip and whether the dough still has strength.
When turned out of the basket
It releases evenly and then flattens, or part of it catches and stretches on the way out.
Note the release separately from the proof. Review dough condition and time in the basket, and check whether it stuck.
After scoring or during transfer
The loaf held shape after release, then opened or slumped during handling.
Check scoring and transfer as well as proof. Have the oven and loading setup ready before turn-out.

blocks.text: A basket supports the loaf during proof, so a loaf can look tall while it is still in the basket. Check whether it releases cleanly and how long it holds its shape after release. A slight relaxation is common. Rapid flattening or obvious tearing gives you a more specific observation to work with. [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-shaping/) [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)
If it spreads on the bench

For a round wheat loaf, use the recipe’s [shaping](/journal/shape-sourdough-boule) method and a bench scraper where helpful. Leave enough friction on the work surface to build tension. If the dough tightens with gentle handling, stop before the surface tears and transfer it to its basket. If it never gathers, check whether it was loose from the first mix or became weaker only towards the end of bulk. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

If it was loose and [sticky](/journal/sourdough-dough-too-sticky) from the first mix after a flour or water change, return to the original flour blend or try one measured water adjustment where the recipe allows. If it started with strength and weakened late, keep the formula and compare actual dough temperature, rise and handling at the end of bulk. That sequence helps separate dough strength from the effect of another tightening pass. [5](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/) [6](https://alexandracooks.com/2020/08/28/why-is-my-sourdough-so-sticky-plus-fixes-to-4-common-sourdough-mistakes-and-faqs/)
If it spreads when you turn it out

If the dough stretches because part of it sticks, first check the basket, liner and dusting recommended for your formula. If it releases smoothly and immediately flattens, compare the condition at shaping with the time and temperature of the final proof. A fragile loaf that looked strong when shaped gives you a different lead from a dough that never held tension on the bench. [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-shaping/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

Imagine two loaves. One begins flattening immediately after final shaping, even before it enters the basket. The second holds on the bench and spreads on release the next morning. Photograph the first at shaping and just before transfer. For the second, photograph the release and record the proof conditions. On the next bake, change the shaping or formula variable supported by the first record. For the second, choose between a release adjustment and a proof adjustment based on what actually happened.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned photo log would keep a shaping photo and a turn-out photo beside the corresponding dough and proof notes. Putting those moments side by side would show whether a flat result began on the bench or only appeared the next day.

title: Why Sourdough Spreads After Shaping
seoTitle: Why Sourdough Spreads After Shaping or Proofing
description: Find out why a shaped sourdough loaf spreads on the bench, sticks during basket release or flattens after turning out.
intro: If sourdough spreads after shaping, identify when it first lost height. A loaf that relaxes on the bench before it goes into the basket calls for a check of dough strength, hydration and shaping tension. A loaf that first spreads when turned out can point to proof, weak tension or dough sticking to the basket. Compare the two moments before deciding what to change. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [2](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-shaping/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

faqs.question: Should I reshape a loaf that spreads after proof?
faqs.answer: If the loaf is already fully proofed and ready for the oven, follow the recipe’s scoring and loading guidance and avoid unnecessary handling. If you are still at preshape and the dough is simply relaxing while holding together, carry on with the planned final shape. The useful question is which stage the loaf is in when you see it spread. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

blocks.text: Start with a formula that expects a same-day bake

The Pantry Mama’s same-day [loaf](/journal/beginner-sourdough-bread-recipe) uses active starter, warm conditions and a counter proof option. Its published [schedule](/journal/sourdough-baking-schedule) starts with a morning mix and leaves the afternoon for shaping, proofing and baking. The author describes a warm proofing setup. A cool kitchen can take substantially longer, even with the same recipe. Use the source recipe for ingredient weights, fold intervals and oven instructions. [1](https://pantrymama.com/same-day-sourdough-bread/)

If you usually feed in the morning and the starter takes several hours to ripen, the real start is later than your feed time. Feed the evening before only if that routine reliably gives you ripe starter when you plan to mix. If the jar still looks early when you wake up, give it time and reconsider the serving target.
An illustrative schedule for a 19:00 dinner

rows: Mix with ripe starter and mark the dough level.
Compare the starter with its normal ripe appearance and record the dough temperature.
Morning
Follow the recipe’s fold sequence and let the dough rest between sets.
It should become more cohesive. Cover it between checks.
Around 13:00
Check bulk and shape when ready.
Look for the recipe’s expansion and aeration cues. Give tight dough another check.
Early to mid-afternoon
Let the covered basket proof at room temperature.
The published counter proof takes around one to two hours in the author’s conditions. Look at the loaf before starting the bake.
Coordinate preheat with final proof and load when both loaf and oven are ready.
This is a planning window. Follow the oven and vessel instructions.
After the bake
Cool the loaf on a rack before slicing.
Judge cooling by the loaf, and reserve more time for a large one.

blocks.text: The clock is an example based on the published method. The source bake takes about 40–45 minutes. If it goes into the oven at 16:00 and comes out around 16:45, a 19:00 dinner gives about two hours and 15 minutes of cooling. Add time if your loaf usually needs longer. [1](https://pantrymama.com/same-day-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

Before the last fold, write down when you can check the dough again. A recipe that needs a late-morning fold is a poor fit if you have to leave then. Put the waiting time after the final planned fold into your calendar as a window, with an earlier check if your dough is warmer than usual.
Pick a latest oven time

Working backwards is easier than trying to recover a late loaf. For this example, allow 45 minutes to bake and two hours to cool. Subtract both from 19:00 and the latest oven load on paper is 16:15. Plan a little earlier for normal variation. Also reserve time before loading for your oven and vessel to preheat.

Now look at the dough at 14:30. If it is still tight in bulk, shaping, final proof and preheating still have to fit before the oven slot. Overlapping preheat with final proof can help when you are home to supervise the oven. It cannot make an underdeveloped loaf ready. If the serving time is fixed, use another loaf for dinner and choose a later bake or a recipe-supported overnight plan. [1](https://pantrymama.com/same-day-sourdough-bread/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake scheduler would let you put in the time you want to slice the bread and reserve the folding, shaping and oven windows. If bulk runs long, you could see how the next check affects serving before trying to squeeze the steps together.
[Read the worked sourdough schedule example](/tools/sourdough-schedule-calculator) with your recipe’s stage durations, then adjust the plan to what your dough shows.

title: A Same-Day Sourdough Baking Schedule
seoTitle: Same-Day Sourdough Baking Schedule for Dinner
description: Plan a morning mix, room-temperature proof and evening sourdough loaf, with a latest oven time that includes cooling.
intro: You can mix, shape and bake sourdough in one day if you start with a ripe starter, use a formula written for same-day baking and leave time for a room-temperature final proof. To serve it that evening, count cooling as part of the schedule. An early mix gives you room to wait if the dough is slower than expected. [1](https://pantrymama.com/same-day-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

faqs.question: Do I need to skip the fridge entirely?
faqs.answer: Choose a formula whose room-temperature final proof is part of its method. If you are following a different recipe with an overnight cold proof, use its stated same-day option or choose a different recipe for that day. A fridge step changes the rest of the timeline. For a more forgiving two-day plan, see the Saturday mix and Sunday bake schedule. [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

blocks.text: Find when the loaf first lost its shape

headers: One check for the next bake
rows: Tight dough and limited expansion before shaping
Starter readiness and the end of bulk.
Record dough temperature and rise from the starting mark. Follow the recipe’s bulk cues.
Dough looked strong at shaping but collapsed on release
Final proof or sticking in the basket.
Record proof time and temperature, then photograph the release before scoring.
Loaf held height on release but tore at an unexpected spot
Scoring, loading and the early bake.
Keep the rest of the method and use one consistent score from the recipe.
Loaf held shape and the cut stayed shallow or barely opened
Preheat, early steam, or the dough’s final proof.
Check how long the vessel and oven had to heat and whether the cover was seated.
Loaf rose well but produced little ear
Loaf shape, score angle and the style of bread.
Compare overall height and crumb before changing fermentation.

blocks.text: These observations narrow the problem. A deep burst is compatible with dough that needed more proof or a score that did not open where intended. A pale, flat loaf can reflect both limited fermentation and oven setup. Use the sequence of events to decide what to test. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2021/02/16/all-about-sourdough-ears) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf) [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)
If it spread before the oven

Compare photos from shaping and basket release. If the loaf never gathered tension, look at how wet the dough was and when it stopped holding together. If it held at shaping but failed after a long proof or tore as it stuck to the liner, the earlier photo helps you separate those possibilities. Work through the bench and basket spread guide before changing the oven. [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

If the dough felt tight before shaping and the cooled slice has a dense base below large tunnels, review the bulk notes. Check the starter’s rise and actual dough temperature. If one of those changed from the last good bake, start there. The [underproofed](/journal/underproofed-vs-overproofed-sourdough) and overproofed comparison shows why the crumb alone gives you a lead rather than a diagnosis. [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf)
If it held shape until loading

Preheat. Follow the recipe’s duration and your equipment limits. Note when the oven signalled temperature and when you loaded. A baking stone or vessel may need longer than the oven’s initial heat-up. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home)

Scoring. Use a clean sharp blade and one purposeful cut appropriate to the loaf shape. On a repeat bake, compare where the cut opened and where the crust burst. Keep the dough and oven method as similar as possible. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2021/02/16/all-about-sourdough-ears)

Steam. A compatible covered baker retains moisture released by the dough during early baking. The uncovered finish lets the crust dry and brown. Use the method your recipe and equipment support. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home)
Take the release photo from the side, from the same distance each time. A top-down picture can show the score but hide whether the loaf already lost height.
Make one comparison worth keeping

Imagine two same-formula loaves. Both release cleanly. In the weaker bake the vessel went in just before loading, while the taller loaf had a full recipe preheat. Preheat is a useful first comparison. If the two loaves also spent different lengths of time in proof, record that difference before drawing a conclusion. On the next bake, reproduce the longer preheat and keep the final-proof conditions comparable.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned [bake journal](/journal/sourdough-bake-journal-template) would keep photos at shaping, release and slicing beside preheat and bake times. You could see whether the loaf lost height before it went in or only failed to open once it was inside.
