title: Why Is My Sourdough Not Getting Oven Spring?
seoTitle: Why Is My Sourdough Not Getting Oven Spring?
description: Find the first point your loaf stopped holding shape, then decide whether to check fermentation, shaping, scoring, steam or preheat.
intro: If sourdough barely rises in the oven, check whether the loaf held its shape before it went in. A loaf that was already tight, weak or spreading points you back to fermentation and shaping. A loaf that held its shape until loading gives you a reason to check preheat, scoring and steam first. A small ear can still sit on a well-risen loaf. Use the loaf’s overall height and cooled crumb as well. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2021/02/16/all-about-sourdough-ears) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/How-to-Read-a-Sourdough-Crumb.pdf)

faqs.question: Does a bigger ear always mean better oven spring?
faqs.answer: A pronounced ear shows how the score opened on that loaf. Judge oven spring by the change in volume, overall profile and cooled crumb. A round loaf scored with a cross can rise well and have a different opening from a loaf with one angled score. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2021/02/16/all-about-sourdough-ears)

targetQuery: why is my sourdough not getting oven spring

blocks.text: What you need for one loaf

rows: Bread flour
White bread flour. Keep the same bag for the first repeat.
Water
Use the source recipe’s temperature guidance.
Ripe sourdough starter
An established starter fed and ready to use. The hydration example below assumes equal weights of flour and water in the starter.
Fine salt
Weigh it. Different salt crystals take up different amounts of space.

blocks.text: The mixed dough weighs about 987 g before handling losses. At 100% starter hydration, the 100 g of starter contributes 50 g flour and 50 g water. That makes the total dough about 77% hydration. A sticky feel early in mixing is expected at this hydration. Use the same formula before trying a water change. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/bakers-percentage)

You will need a digital scale, mixing bowl, covered straight-sided container, scraper, round basket or towel-lined bowl, suitable covered baker, oven gloves and a cooling rack. Check the vessel, lid and any parchment against the temperatures in the recipe. Keep the path between the counter and oven clear before the pot is hot. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home)
Day one from starter to basket
1. Check the starter and mix

Use starter that has risen predictably after a feed and looks airy and expanded, according to the feeding routine you know. If it is still tight and low in the jar, wait for its normal cues. There is no useful reason to lock in a mix time if the starter has yet to ripen. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/)

Stir the starter into the water. Add the flour and salt and mix until no pockets of dry flour remain. Scrape the sides and cover the dough. Mark its starting level in the [bulk](/journal/when-is-bulk-fermentation-done) container so you can compare the same batch later. Let the dough rest about 30 minutes before the first [folds](/journal/stretch-and-fold-sourdough). [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/)
2. Fold and track bulk

Over the first two hours, the source method describes up to four fold sets at roughly 30-minute intervals. For each set, lift a section and fold it over the middle, then rotate the container and repeat around the dough. Use lightly damp hands. Stop a pull when the dough resists. By later sets it should feel more cohesive and sit higher after you let it go. The stretch and fold guide shows what to look for. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-stretch-and-fold-sourdough-bread-dough/)

After the folds, let the dough continue developing in the covered tub. In this method, look for roughly half again the initial volume alongside a more aerated feel. Use the marked container and the dough together. If the dough is cooler or the starter less active, it can take longer than your schedule. Avoid shaping a tight mass simply because a timer has ended. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [5](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)
3. Preshape, rest and shape

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface as the method directs. Gather it into a round with light, short movements. Let it rest, then tighten it into its final round. The dough should be easier to shape after a short bench rest. If it tears instead of tightening, reduce the pull and check how it behaved in bulk. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [6](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/)

Place the dough seam side up in the prepared basket. Cover and refrigerate as the source method directs. For an ordinary overnight plan, the published recipe suggests about 12–18 hours as a starting interval, with longer options for this formula. Write down the actual time and the condition at shaping so the morning plan has a real starting point. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/)
Day two from basket to rack
4. Preheat and load

Stafford’s method heats the oven and compatible Dutch oven at 450°F (about 232°C), with at least 45 minutes of heating for the pot. Only use that preheat when your vessel permits it. Release the cold loaf onto your prepared loading surface, score it and load it promptly. Have the hot lid and the landing area for it planned ahead. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home)
5. Bake, uncover and cool

Bake covered for about 30 minutes in the source method, then remove the lid, reduce to 400°F (about 204°C), and finish for about 10–15 minutes. Check the recipe’s colour cues and allow the loaf to finish baking before removing it. Move it to a rack and let it cool before slicing. The recipe allows about an hour. A larger loaf or a still-warm centre may need longer. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [7](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

rows: End of mix
Dough temperature and the starting mark.
Last fold
How well the mass lifts and holds together.
Shaping
Expansion and how aerated or tight the dough feels.
Basket release
Whether the round releases cleanly and keeps its profile.
After cooling
A centre slice, texture and what you would try again.

blocks.text: [Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would let you keep those observations next to your recipe and actual times. If the next loaf behaves differently, you can compare a particular step with the first loaf instead of starting over.
Give yourself a checkpoint on each day

On the first day, reserve the opening two hours for mixing and the early folds, then leave a wider window for bulk and shaping. Check whether you can be home when the dough is ready. On the second day, allow for the full preheat, the covered and uncovered bake and cooling before anyone expects a slice. A printed clock is helpful for appointments. Use the dough and recipe to decide when to move between them.
[Read the sourdough hydration formula and example](/tools/sourdough-hydration-calculator) to include the flour and water in your starter without counting them twice.

title: A Beginner Sourdough Bread Recipe in Grams
seoTitle: Beginner Sourdough Bread Recipe in Grams
description: Make one white-flour sourdough loaf with weighed ingredients and checkpoints from ripe starter through cooling.
intro: For a first sourdough loaf, start with 500 g bread flour, 375 g water, 100 g ripe starter and 12 g salt. This one-loaf guide follows the ingredient choices in Alexandra Stafford’s published white-flour sourdough method. Mix and fold on day one, refrigerate the shaped round, and bake on day two. The most useful skill on the first attempt is knowing what to look for at each stage. [1](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/)

faqs.question: What if the loaf is flat or gummy?
faqs.answer: If the loaf spread on release, compare its condition at shaping and after final proof. If it feels gummy after a full cool, check the bake and note where the sticky areas are. Use the gummy crumb guide or the oven spring guide to choose one change. Keep the original formula and the parts of the process you can reproduce. One repeat with good notes teaches more about your own kitchen than changing the flour, water, starter and baking time together.

blocks.text: Do one set without tearing the dough

items: Let the mixed dough rest for the period in your recipe. Put the bowl on a steady surface and lightly dampen your hand.
Slide your fingers under one edge. Lift slowly until the dough stretches and you feel resistance.
Lay that section across the centre. Turn the bowl about a quarter-turn.
Repeat at the other sides. Cover the dough again and record the time if you are following a schedule.

blocks.text: The goal is a smoother, more cohesive mass. You might make four moves in a set, one from each side, and need a shorter lift on the last move because the dough has tightened. Forcing every lift to the same height can tear the dough. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-stretch-and-fold-sourdough-bread-dough/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)
How many sets does this loaf need?

Look up your recipe first. The Perfect [Loaf](/journal/beginner-sourdough-bread-recipe)’s beginner recipe uses three early sets separated by roughly half an hour. Other methods use different mixing, rest and fold patterns. A strong mix may need less handling than a slack dough that is relying on folds for development. Write down what your recipe expects before starting bulk. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

rows: Dough clings to your fingers but lifts as one piece
Lightly dampen your hand and keep the movement steady.
Dough tightens quickly and holds itself together
Shorten the stretch and let it rest.
Dough tears on a long pull
Reduce the lift. Look at whether it was already strong or unusually weak.
Dough is puffy late in bulk
Follow the recipe’s readiness cues and avoid adding folds just to fill time.

blocks.text: Fold timing and bulk readiness answer different questions. A completed set tells you the dough has had that handling. Expansion and aeration tell you about its progress towards [shaping](/journal/shape-sourdough-boule). Keep those observations separate. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [3](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

If the first set felt loose and the third felt smooth, note what changed. [Crispy Crust](/)’s planned fold reminders would sit alongside bake notes, so you could record how a set felt and compare it with the same step on the next loaf.

If you miss a scheduled fold, check how far into bulk you are and how the dough feels. Early in bulk, a recipe may have time for another set. Once the dough is well aerated near shaping, avoid trying to make up all the missed handling in one go. Write down the change for your next bake.

sources.label: The Perfect Loaf · Stretch and folds

title: How to Stretch and Fold Sourdough
seoTitle: How to Stretch and Fold Sourdough Dough
description: Learn one four-sided fold set, how to handle tight or sticky dough and when to stop folding during bulk.
intro: To stretch and fold sourdough, lift one side of the dough until it starts to resist, lay it over the centre, and rotate the bowl. Repeat around the dough to complete a set. Use lightly damp hands and keep the dough covered between sets. Follow the recipe’s intervals, then use the dough’s strength to judge how gently to handle it. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-stretch-and-fold-sourdough-bread-dough/) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

faqs.question: Is a coil fold different?
faqs.answer: A coil fold typically lifts the dough from underneath so its ends tuck under. A stretch and fold brings an edge over the centre. Follow the technique your recipe was written around while you learn its feel. A sticky dough check can help when you cannot tell whether the dough needs support or simply a gentler touch. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-stretch-and-fold-sourdough-bread-dough/)

targetQuery: how to stretch and fold sourdough

blocks.text: Preshape to give the dough a starting form

Turn out the dough when bulk is ready. Use a scraper to gather the dough and guide it into a rough round. If your recipe makes two loaves, divide before gathering each piece. Aim for a smooth surface you can handle later. A preshape only needs enough tension to keep the dough together through its rest. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2018/05/31/shaping-a-boule) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

Give the dough the bench rest in your recipe. The Perfect [Loaf](/journal/beginner-sourdough-bread-recipe)’s beginner method gives about 25 minutes. Watch for a little relaxation. If the dough springs back and feels tight, it may need time to relax. If it flattens fast and loses its edges, look at the strength it had in bulk before trying another tightening move. [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/) [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/)
Build surface tension in the final shape

items: Prepare the basket first so the finished round has somewhere to go.
Flip the rested dough as your recipe directs. Fold sections towards the centre to bring it together.
Turn the package seam side down. With cupped hands or a scraper, draw the round gently towards you over a surface with enough grip to tighten it.
Rotate a little and repeat only while the skin is smoothing without tearing.

Transfer to the basket in the orientation your bake method uses. For a round to be inverted for scoring, this is commonly seam side up. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [3](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/beginners-sourdough-bread/)

headers: What happens during the last pull
rows: The surface smooths and the round stays tall
Stop tightening and transfer it.
The whole round slides with no grip
Clear some excess bench flour from the area used to tighten it.
The surface snags or tears
Release it with a scraper and use less force. Check the dough’s strength.
It tightens briefly then quickly flows
Look back at mixing and bulk. A second pull may give little lasting support.

blocks.text: A tight skin comes from the movement of the dough against the bench. Pushing hard with your fingers can pinch or tear it. For a sticky but cohesive dough, use the scraper to release the edge and start again with a shorter movement. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned bake log would put the preshape and final-shape photos beside the timing and dough notes. That would help you see whether the round was already [spreading](/journal/sourdough-spreads-after-shaping) before it went into the basket.

For your next loaf, take one side photo after the preshape and another from the same spot after the bench rest. If it relaxed slightly and remained rounded, the rest did its job. If it already flattened, your photos can narrow the problem to the earlier dough or preshape, before the final tightening pass.

sources.label: The Perfect Loaf · Shaping a boule

title: How to Shape a Round Sourdough Boule
seoTitle: How to Shape a Round Sourdough Boule
description: Preshape, rest and shape a round sourdough loaf with enough surface tension to hold together without tearing.
intro: Shape a sourdough boule by first gathering the dough into a rough round, letting it relax, then tightening its surface with short, gentle movements. Stop when the round holds together and the surface feels taut. If it tears, the pull has gone too far for that dough. Put the finished round into its prepared basket and begin final proof. [1](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/shaping-a-boule/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2018/05/31/shaping-a-boule)

faqs.question: Where does shaping end and proofing begin?
faqs.answer: After the final round is in its proofing basket or other support, you are in final proof. Follow the room-temperature or fridge instructions in the recipe. If the loaf looks good in the basket but spreads when you turn it out, compare the bench and basket release checks before changing your final-shape technique. [4](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)

targetQuery: how to shape a sourdough boule

blocks.text: Split the starter into flour and water first

Starter hydration is the weight of water divided by the weight of flour, multiplied by 100. Equal weights of flour and water give 100% hydration. A stiff starter at 60% hydration contains 60 g water for every 100 g flour. A [scale](/journal/scale-sourdough-recipe) tells you the weight of the combined starter, so work backwards to find the two components. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/reference/introduction-to-bakers-percentages/)
Starter flour = starter weight ÷ (1 + starter hydration ÷ 100).
Starter water = starter weight − starter flour.
Total hydration (%) = (added water + starter water) ÷ (added flour + starter flour) × 100.

Use the same weight units throughout. Enter the starter hydration as 100 for an equal-weight starter or 60 for a 60% starter. Count only the starter that goes into the dough. The part left in the mother jar has no effect on this calculation.
Two examples with the same 120 g of starter

rows: Added flour and water
500 g flour and 350 g water
500 g flour and 350 g water
Flour in 120 g starter
Water in 120 g starter
Total flour and water
560 g flour and 410 g water
575 g flour and 395 g water
Total hydration

blocks.text: Both columns have the same added-water percentage of 70%. The liquid starter increases total hydration above that figure, while the stiffer starter brings it below. Replacing starter by weight can therefore change a dough even if the added water and flour never move.
Check what the recipe already counts

A recipe card may show a final-dough mix with a separate levain line. In that case, add the levain’s flour and water once. A total formula may already include flour and water from the levain. In that case, divide the stated totals directly. If the recipe has a separate levain build, use the hydration of the portion that actually goes into the dough, especially if it differs from the mother jar. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/reference/introduction-to-bakers-percentages/)

Check your feed notes if the starter hydration is uncertain. The ratio of your last flour and water additions is a useful clue, but the old seed also contributes flour and water. For a new build made from a large proportion of seed, include its contribution. If you lack those weights, label the result an estimate.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned recipe tools would keep the starter hydration beside the ingredient weights. That would help you compare formulas with the same denominator and catch a change when you switch from a liquid starter to a stiff one.
Add up more than one preferment

If you add two builds, split each at its own hydration and sum their flour and water separately. For example, 100 g of equal-weight starter gives 50 g of each, while 80 g at 60% hydration gives 50 g flour and 30 g water. Together they contribute 100 g flour and 80 g water. Keep those lines separate in your notes so you can audit the total.
[Read the sourdough hydration formula and example](/tools/sourdough-hydration-calculator) to include the flour and water in your starter without counting them twice.

title: How to Calculate Sourdough Hydration Including the Starter
seoTitle: How to Calculate Sourdough Hydration With Starter
description: Include flour and water from a liquid or stiff starter in sourdough hydration, with two checked examples.
intro: To calculate total sourdough hydration, add the water in your starter to the recipe water and the flour in your starter to the recipe flour. Divide total water by total flour and multiply by 100. With 500 g flour, 350 g water and 120 g of 100% hydration starter, the result is 73.2% total hydration. The added-water figure for the same dough is 70%. Both are useful if you label the convention. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/bakers-percentage) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/reference/introduction-to-bakers-percentages/)

faqs.question: Why does my 73% dough feel different from another 73% dough?
faqs.answer: Hydration describes the weight ratio. Flour blend, absorption, rest, mixing and fermentation affect how that water feels in the dough. Compare like with like before deciding it needs more flour or less water. If the number is clear but the dough is difficult to handle, see the sticky dough guide. [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2020/11/05/how-to-produce-an-open-crumb-in-sourdough-bread)

targetQuery: how to calculate sourdough hydration including starter

blocks.text: Start with a formula you can read both ways

rows: Added flour
Added water
Starter at 100% hydration
Salt
Total dough

blocks.text: The total is 192% because the denominator is the flour alone. This convention makes a final mix easy to weigh. The starter’s percentage is its full 100 g divided by the 500 g flour you add at mixing. It is a convenient description of the formula’s ingredient lines.
Include the starter when comparing total formulas

The 100 g of equal-weight starter contains 50 g flour and 50 g water. The same dough contains 550 g flour and 400 g water in total. On that denominator, total [hydration](/journal/calculate-sourdough-hydration-with-starter) is 72.7% and salt is about 1.82%. Prefermented flour is 50 ÷ 550, or about 9.1%. That figure describes the flour that arrived already fermented. It answers a different question from the 20% starter weight in the final-mix table. [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/reference/introduction-to-bakers-percentages/)

rows: How much starter do I weigh?
20% of 500 g added flour gives 100 g.
What is the total hydration?
400 g total water ÷ 550 g total flour = 72.7%.
How much flour is prefermented?
50 g starter flour ÷ 550 g total flour = 9.1%.

blocks.text: Do the conversion once. If the recipe’s total flour already includes the [levain](/journal/levain-vs-starter), adding the levain flour again makes the denominator too large. If the build uses a stiff starter, the starter split formula gives the correct amount to add.
Go from percentages to grams

Choose a flour weight and convert each percentage to a decimal before multiplying. To use the final-mix table with 600 g added flour, multiply 600 by 0.70 for 420 g water, by 0.20 for 120 g starter and by 0.02 for 12 g salt. The new dough weighs 1,152 g. Keep the starter at the same hydration for that conversion. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/bakers-percentage)

If you are aiming for a specific dough weight, divide that weight by 1.92 to find the added flour weight for this convention. For example, 1,056 g ÷ 1.92 gives 550 g added flour. The ingredient amounts become 550 g flour, 385 g water, 110 g starter and 11 g salt. If the scale rounds small amounts, keep the rounding visible. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/bakers-percentage)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned formula view would show the gram weights and their percentage convention side by side. That could help you spot a changed denominator before you copy a formula into your next bake.
Combine flours without losing the denominator

If the 500 g of added flour is made from 400 g white and 100 g whole wheat, write those as 80% and 20% on the added-flour denominator. They add to 100%. Water and salt percentages still use the combined 500 g. For a total-flour comparison, include the type of flour in the starter too. With a 50 g white-flour contribution, this dough has 100 g whole wheat out of 550 g total flour, or 18.2%. Label both lines if you will use them for different jobs. This also makes comparisons easier.
[Read the sourdough hydration formula and example](/tools/sourdough-hydration-calculator) to include the flour and water in your starter without counting them twice.

title: Baker’s Percentages for Sourdough
seoTitle: Baker’s Percentages for Sourdough With Examples
description: Use flour as 100%, convert sourdough percentages to grams and distinguish starter percentage from prefermented flour.
intro: In baker’s percentages, flour is always 100% because every ingredient is expressed as a percentage of the flour weight. If a recipe has 500 g flour and 350 g water, the water is 70% of the flour weight. In sourdough, a formula can count flour in the starter separately or include it in the 100%. Write down which convention you are using before you compare recipes. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/bakers-percentage) [2](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/reference/introduction-to-bakers-percentages/)

faqs.question: Which convention should I write on my recipe card?
faqs.answer: Use the ingredient list people will weigh and label its flour denominator. Add a total hydration line if you compare recipes with different starters or levains. If someone else needs to recreate the dough, include the starter hydration so they can recover both sets of numbers.

blocks.text: Score the app with one real feed

rows: Logging speed
Enter starter, flour and water in grams, plus time. Edit an incorrect entry without replacing your whole history.
Reminder control
Change the next feed after an early feed. Check recurring schedules, snooze and what happens when the starter goes into the fridge.
Observations
Save a starting mark, a later rise reading and the relevant temperature. See whether they sit with the same feed.
History and export
Find an older entry and check how much history is available. Try exporting a sample record in a format you can open elsewhere.
Cost and privacy
Check the tier you need, whether an account is required, and where the app says photos and notes are stored.

blocks.text: If an app has multiple starter profiles, use them only when you actually keep different cultures or maintenance routines. Separate a rye starter from a wheat one so the histories mean something. A one-jar routine can be simpler. The printable [feeding log](/journal/sourdough-starter-feeding-log) gives you a way to test the fields you use before you commit to an app.
Compare what the listings actually describe
The examples below are from UK App Store listings checked 10 November 2026. Treat listed features as developer descriptions and check the app on the device and tier you would use.

headers: What to verify during a trial
rows: Loaflo
Feed logging, hydration and growth tracking. Its release notes mention starter reminders and Pro bake schedules. [1](https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/loaflo-sourdough-starter/id6736766728)
Whether reminders fit your routine and whether history or exports meet your needs.
Surdeg

Recurring reminders per starter, feeding history, a bake journal and local storage. The listing describes premium limits for some history and multiple starters. [2](https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/surdeg-sourdough-tracker/id6766092580)
What is included on your tier and how you would retain a copy of your data.

blocks.text: For Android, check the exact developer name before installing. Google Play has several apps with similar names. The listing for Sourdough Tracker identifies the app by its package and explains its own tracking features. Read the device and availability details on the store page, then run the same test. [3](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sourdoughtracker)
Check whether your history changes a decision

After three comparable feeds, ask whether you can find the one that peaked earliest. Can you tell whether it was warmer, fed at a different ratio or recorded at a different time? An app that only says you fed on Tuesday may cover the reminder job. A feed log with observations can help you decide how early to build a levain for a Saturday loaf.

Try this sequence once before you pay. Log a feed, add a height observation, adjust the next reminder and retrieve both records the next day. If you use two devices, check whether the records appear where you expect. If you care about keeping your own archive, make a sample export and open it. An export option has more value when the file includes the weights, time and notes you need.

[Crispy Crust](/) is upcoming. Its planned starter log connects feed weights and rise observations to bake planning, so you could use the history to decide when to build your levain. Treat the plan as a preview and use the store listings to compare tools you can try now.
Choose a trial that matches the problem

If you mainly miss feeds, try a reminder through a real change in routine. Record an early feed and check whether the next alert follows the new time. If the main problem is inconsistent rise, record three comparable feeds before judging the history view. A photo is more useful if the starting level and time sit next to it. Before subscribing, check whether the tier you tried is the one that includes the features you used. Keep a note of any limitations you hit during the trial.

faqs.question: Do I need an app if I only feed once a week?
faqs.answer: A calendar reminder and a short paper log may be enough. An app becomes more useful if feeding times move, you manage several jars or you want to compare feeds with the loaves they produced. Start with the smallest record you can keep consistently.

blocks.text: Find when the crust lost its crunch

rows: Soon after leaving the oven
Whether the uncovered finish was long enough for the recipe’s colour and doneness cues.
Keep the same formula and record the uncovered time and crust colour.
While cooling on a board or tray
Whether air could circulate under the loaf.
Use a rack and compare the underside after a full cool.
After wrapping or storing
Whether you enclosed the loaf while it was warm, or used a bag that kept moisture against the crust.
Cool fully first. Compare the crust before wrapping and the next day.
It is soft outside and tacky in the middle
Whether the crumb actually cooled and the bake finished.
Use the gummy crumb guide to assess the centre separately.

blocks.text: Moisture from the crumb can soften the crust as the [loaf](/journal/beginner-sourdough-bread-recipe) cools and sits. Early steam can help a loaf expand, and a drier finish helps the crust firm. Follow the timing for your bake and note when you uncovered the loaf. A very dark crust with a tacky centre calls for a review of the oven and recipe together. [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home) [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)
Change cooling first if the bake already looks right

Put the loaf on a rack with enough room beneath it, and leave it uncovered until fully cool. Compare the base and top at the same time. A base that softened while sitting against a flat surface gives you a specific observation to repeat with a rack. If both surfaces softened before storage, look back at how the crust coloured in the uncovered phase.

For storage, decide what you care about most. An airtight wrap can preserve crumb moisture and also soften a crisp crust. If you want to keep part of a loaf for longer, let it cool, freeze what you will not use and reheat portions as needed. Follow the storage and refreshing method for the loaf you made. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/11/06/how-to-store-sourdough-bread)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned [bake journal](/journal/sourdough-bake-journal-template) would let you keep lid-off time, cooling setup and the crust’s texture next morning beside the recipe. That would make it easier to tell whether a repeat bake improved the crust or whether only the storage changed.

For a controlled comparison, use two loaves from the same recipe and record when each left the oven. To isolate storage, cool both fully on a rack and check that the crusts feel comparable before wrapping them differently. Check both again after the same interval. If one loaf was wrapped warm, the trial also changed cooling, so log that as a separate difference.

description: Find out why sourdough crust softens while cooling or after wrapping and what to change for a crisper crust.
intro: If sourdough crust goes soft while the loaf cools, start with the uncovered bake and how you cool the loaf. blocks.text: Use a rimmed metal sheet pan that fits the oven and fridge shelf. A smaller pan gives a thicker layer for the same amount of dough. For a 9 × 13 inch pan, the source explicitly supports making a half batch. If you plan to use a different pan, check its dimensions before mixing. Two pans with similar labels can have different interior areas and depths. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)

Make enough ripe starter without emptying the jar you maintain. A 340 g recipe portion is larger than many feeding jars. Build the quantity ahead of time using your normal starter routine. If it is still low and tight when you want to start, delay the mix and move the fridge target with it. The [small starter guide](/journal/low-discard-sourdough-starter) shows how to work backwards from the amount needed.
Day one from mixing to the fridge
1. Mix and develop the dough

Stir the ripe starter into the water, then add the flour, dough oil, salt and honey. Mix until the dry flour disappears. The source method kneads until the dough is elastic and smooth. It estimates about 5–7 minutes in a mixer on its lowest speed or 12–15 minutes by hand. Treat those as checks for that method. If you use a mixer, stay within its dough capacity and speed guidance. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)

Cover the dough in a lightly oiled bowl. In the published schedule it rises for about an hour, gets a gentle fold, then rises for about another hour. Look at the mass before and after the fold. A dough that starts to feel smoother and holds together is easier to move into the pan without pulling it thin in one spot. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)
2. Stretch the dough into the oiled tray

Oil the tray as the recipe directs and turn the dough in the oil. Spread it gently from the centre out. If it pulls back before reaching the corners, cover it, wait 10–15 minutes and try again. Rest lets you make progress with less force. Look across the pan for large differences in thickness rather than dragging a thin edge to fill the last corner. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)

When it fills the pan, cover it and refrigerate it for the recipe’s 14–16 hours. Record the time the tray went in. As a worked example, a tray chilled at 19:00 can come out at 10:00 after 15 hours. Let it sit during preheat as the recipe directs. This clock is an illustration of the published range. The condition of the dough and fridge matters more than an exact appointment on the minute. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)
Day two from tray proof to a baked focaccia
3. Check the tray before dimpling

Take the tray out while the oven preheats to 425°F (about 218°C). The recipe allows roughly 30–60 minutes depending on kitchen warmth. Check that the dough looks aerated and has relaxed into its corners. Look for a soft, puffy surface. If it still feels tight and shows little development, compare the starter, room conditions and the published cues before proceeding. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)

blocks.text: 4. Dimple, top and bake

Use oiled fingers to press into the dough at intervals. Make wells across the tray without repeatedly pressing the same area. Drizzle with oil and finish with rosemary and flaky salt as the source directs. Keep toppings simple on the first run so you can see how the crust and centre bake. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)

Bake for about 20–25 minutes in the published method. Look for a light golden surface, then let the tray cool enough to handle safely before transferring the focaccia to a rack. Inspect the centre as well as the edges. A thin corner can colour before the middle. Record the colour you saw when you took it out and the texture after a short cool. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)

title: Overnight Sourdough Focaccia in a Sheet Pan
seoTitle: Overnight Sourdough Focaccia in a Sheet Pan
description: Make sourdough focaccia with an overnight tray proof, exact ingredient weights and cues for dimpling and baking.
intro: Sourdough focaccia is ready to dimple when the dough has spread across the oiled pan, looks puffy and gives a little when pressed. Dimple just before baking. This guide follows King Arthur Baking’s published overnight focaccia, which uses ripe starter and a 13 × 18 inch rimmed half-sheet pan. The dough rises in the pan in the fridge for 14–16 hours, then rests at room temperature while the oven heats. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-focaccia-recipe)

faqs.question: Can I use a round tin instead?
faqs.answer: Choose a tested formula for the tin if you want predictable thickness and bake time. For this formula, start with the published half-sheet or the supported half batch in a 9 × 13 inch pan. When you repeat the bake, compare the same part of the tray in your photos. A centre piece and a corner piece can tell different stories.

blocks.text: Why remove part of the starter?

A feed adds flour and water. Removing a portion keeps the jar at a manageable size and gives you control over how much fresh flour and water the remaining culture gets. For example, if a jar holds 120 g and you retain 30 g for its next feed, the 90 g you removed is discard. The 30 g you keep goes back into the regular [feeding routine](/journal/feed-sourdough-starter). [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/18/sourdough-discard)

The word describes what you did with that portion. It does not tell you how long it has been sitting, how much it has risen or how well it can raise dough. Label those details separately. That distinction matters if you are choosing between a loaf and a [pancake](/journal/sourdough-discard-pancakes) recipe.
Choose the recipe by what the starter needs to do

rows: Ripe starter as the main leavener
A fed, active starter that meets the recipe’s cues.
A separate levain build
Make the build and wait for the stated ripeness before mixing.
Unfed discard in pancakes with baking powder
Use suitable discard at the specified hydration. The baking powder supplies lift in that formula.
Unfed discard in thin crackers
Use the amount specified and bake fully. The cracker method depends on even thickness and drying.
Discard in a bread recipe with added yeast
Follow that specific formula. The yeast supplies leavening the recipe was designed around.

blocks.text: The same-day pancake guide and discard cracker guide use the same ingredient for different jobs. Crackers get their texture from rolling thin and baking through. Pancakes get lift from baking powder and heat. Either recipe can use discard without waiting for it to reach a bread starter’s peak. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/18/sourdough-discard) [3](https://www.thisjess.com/sourdough-discard-pancakes/) [4](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-crackers-recipe)
Can you swap discard for ripe starter?

Check the recipe’s leavening first. Cold or older discard may be less active than the ripe starter the loaf expects. A better route is to feed a sound portion and use it when it reaches the recipe’s cues. For a discard recipe, match the weights and starter hydration. At 100% hydration, 100 g contributes 50 g of flour and 50 g of water. That matters if you are adapting a recipe, even when rise comes from baking powder or commercial yeast. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/18/sourdough-discard)

Do not taste raw discard. It contains raw flour, which needs cooking. Discard from a starter that is still becoming established should be thrown away until your starter method says it is established and suitable to use. Throw away contaminated starter and related discard. [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [5](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned feed log would separate what you keep for the next feed from what you remove. That would help you see how much discard you actually have without counting the starter you need for your next loaf.
[Read the discard recipe quantity examples](/tools/discard-recipe-finder) and compare the original recipes before choosing what to make.

title: What Is Sourdough Discard?
seoTitle: What Is Sourdough Discard and When Can You Use It?
description: Learn what sourdough discard is, when to use it and when a recipe needs ripe starter instead.
intro: Sourdough discard is the portion you remove from your starter before feeding what remains. It still contains flour, water and the starter culture. Use discard from a healthy, established starter in recipes written for it. A recipe that relies on ripe starter to raise a loaf needs starter with the activity that method expects. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/18/sourdough-discard) [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

blocks.text: Label the discard separately from the starter

items: Before feeding, check the established starter and use a clean utensil. Transfer the portion you want to keep for cooking into a clean food container.
Write the date and, if you bake by weight, the grams and usual starter hydration. Mark the container “discard” so you do not confuse it with the starter you feed.
Keep it covered and chilled. If you collect several feeds in one container, keep the earliest date and note the total weight. A new addition does not make older discard fresh.

Take out what the recipe needs using a clean utensil. Plan the recipe before the jar becomes hard to date. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/18/sourdough-discard) [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

rows: Collected 10 Nov
You can trace the oldest portion.
120 g, equal-weight flour and water starter
You can compare it with the recipe’s amount and hydration.
Mother starter in a separate jar
You know which culture still needs regular feeds.

blocks.text: How long does it last in the fridge?

There is no single fridge life that covers every jar. King Arthur gives storage and quality guidance for [discard](/journal/what-is-sourdough-discard), while Colorado State University Extension explains how to recognise suspect starter and handle raw flour. The date, handling and storage conditions matter. Use the oldest dated portion promptly and choose a recipe appropriate for the discard you have. If you are uncertain about the history or see [signs of contamination](/journal/sourdough-starter-mold), throw it away. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/18/sourdough-discard) [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/) [3](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)

A layer of liquid can form on starter. Colorado State distinguishes an alcoholic-smelling liquid from coloured or fuzzy mould. If growth looks suspect or you are unsure which it is, discard the batch. If the mother jar showed mould, discard the starter and any discard collected from it. Clean the equipment thoroughly. [2](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/sourdough-starter-best-practices/)

If you know your next recipe uses 200 g, write that target on the lid. It helps you see when you have enough without mixing in another undated portion. Use a separate clean container for a new collection if the older batch has an uncertain history.
Can I freeze discard?

Some baking guides use freezing to store discard for later cooked recipes. Portion it in a freezer-safe container, label the date and grams and follow the recipe’s thawing guidance. Freezing does not make raw flour ready to eat or make a suspect batch usable. Use a fresh feeding routine if you need reliably ripe starter for bread. [4](https://www.cravethegood.com/how-to-store-sourdough-discard/) [3](https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/handling-flour-safely-what-you-need-know)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned starter and discard notes would help you link a measured portion to its collection date and source feed. That gives you a more useful record than a jar you have been topping up without dates. When you want to use it, start with the discard recipes by amount grid.

This guide follows the stone-or-steel and baking-shell setup demonstrated by King Arthur. It works with a covered first phase and an uncovered finish. Choose a published [loaf](/journal/beginner-sourdough-bread-recipe) method that supports your setup and use the manufacturer’s limits for the exact equipment you own. Finish uncovered and look for the recipe’s browning and doneness cues. Move the loaf to a rack to cool. Avoid pouring water onto oven glass, the oven floor or hot cookware for a method that does not call for it. If you lack compatible equipment, choose a bread recipe and pan you can use within their instructions. [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home) [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/02/27/covered-baker-bread-steaming)

Take a note of the actual preheat, covered and uncovered times. Record whether the loaf held its shape after release and which part browned first. If it spreads before loading, compare shaping and proof before blaming the shell. If it holds but turns out pale and flat, check the heat and cover fit on the next attempt. Rehearse the handoff before you preheat

With cold equipment, check where the shell handle sits when the oven door is open. Put the landing surface close enough that you can move the cover there in one motion. Check that your peel or other loading tool fits the rack height and that your mitts let you grip the cover securely. If you cannot lift it clear without tilting it towards you, adjust the rack while everything is cold or choose a different setup. description: Use a compatible baking shell and stone or steel for sourdough, with equipment checks and safe loading guidance.
intro: You can bake sourdough without a Dutch oven using an oven-safe bread-baking shell over a compatible baking stone or steel. The shell holds moisture released by the dough during the first part of the bake. Use a shell designed for that job and follow the temperature, preheating and loading instructions for both pieces and for your oven. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/02/27/covered-baker-bread-steaming) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2024/04/26/baking-bread-with-steam-at-home)

faqs.answer: Use a recipe that is written for that setup. A tray alone gives the loaf a place to bake, while the recipe has to account for how the crust sets and how the loaf is shaped or supported. Check its specific loading instructions before heating the oven. If you want the covered-steam effect without a Dutch oven, use the compatible shell method above. blocks.text: Start with the weight before baking

Use the amount of dough you want to divide at the bench. A baked loaf weighs less because it loses moisture during baking. If a recipe gives only a baked weight, total the weights of the ingredients that actually go into the dough. Count only the levain used in the dough, and leave out bench flour, basket flour and the starter reserve.
Scale factor = target dough weight ÷ original dough weight.
New ingredient weight = original ingredient weight × scale factor.

blocks.text: Use the full factor during calculation. Round only when you decide what to weigh. In this example both rounding plans sum to the target. If your individual rounded lines leave a one-gram difference, note it or apply a small adjustment to a larger ingredient. Avoid putting the entire correction into a small salt or yeast quantity. Check the mixed dough after bowl losses and divide it into two equal portions by weight. [1](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/bakers-percentage)

If you need to build a levain, calculate the amount the scaled dough uses and then plan the build and reserve. A 177 g starter line means the dough needs 177 g of starter at the same [hydration](/journal/calculate-sourdough-hydration-with-starter) and ripeness. It does not tell you how much should stay in the mother jar. The [small starter guide](/journal/low-discard-sourdough-starter) covers that separate calculation.
Batch size can move the schedule

A bigger batch needs enough space in the mixing bowl and bulk tub. If you use a mixer, check its dough capacity. The extra dough can cool or warm at a different rate, so check the actual dough temperature and watch the recipe’s bulk cues. Doubling dough weight gives you more dough. The recipe’s clock does not double with it. [3](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/pro/reference/dough-temperature) [4](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)

Decide how the loaves fit in the oven. If you have one covered vessel, plan separate oven appointments and a supported way to hold the second loaf. The two-loaf schedule shows where to put the recovery time and when to check each loaf.

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned recipe scaler would let you set the number of loaves and target dough weight, then retain the original formula alongside the scaled version. That would make it easier to check that a changed gram weight came from the scale factor.
Check a small batch before rounding

Scaling the same 960 g formula down to 480 g gives 250 g flour, 175 g water, 50 g starter and 5 g salt. Smaller batches can make a scale’s resolution more noticeable, especially for salt. If the scale cannot reliably show a small quantity, use one with an appropriate resolution or make a batch size you can weigh. If you need a whole number of portions, calculate the target total first so you can weigh each one consistently.

intro: To scale sourdough, divide your target total dough weight by the original total dough weight, then multiply each ingredient by that factor. faqs.answer: Use the same formula and oven setup to measure your own bake loss after cooling. If a previous 850 g dough portion cooled to 740 g, it retained about 87.1% of its dough weight. That gives you a planning estimate for a comparable loaf. Actual loss can change with loaf shape, finish and cooling. Start by scaling the raw portions to the same weight and checking both loaves after cooling.

Use a starter that is ripe according to your feeding method. Combine it with the recipe water, then mix in both flours and the salt until the flour is moistened. Let the covered dough rest for about 30 minutes as the source method directs. A wholemeal dough can feel coarser than a white dough at first. Check it again after the rest before deciding the water amount needs to change. [1](https://simmeringstarfruit.com/2026/02/22/whole-wheat-sourdough-bread/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2020/11/05/how-to-produce-an-open-crumb-in-sourdough-bread)
2. Fold and judge bulk

The source 50/50 option uses four early fold sets about half an hour apart. Use a shorter pull when the dough resists. Whole wheat flour can make the dough feel different from the white loaf even at similar hydration. Look for how it stretches and holds together across sets, then let it continue developing after the last fold. [1](https://simmeringstarfruit.com/2026/02/22/whole-wheat-sourdough-bread/) [5](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/how-to-stretch-and-fold-sourdough-bread-dough/)

Use visible expansion, bubbles and a more aerated feel to assess bulk. The source describes a dough that looks larger and moves more lightly in its container. Track actual dough temperature and the rise from your starting mark if you can. Use the combination rather than relying on a sample that floats. If your dough has limited expansion and feels tight, schedule another check before shaping. [1](https://simmeringstarfruit.com/2026/02/22/whole-wheat-sourdough-bread/) [6](https://thesourdoughjourney.com/faq-bulk-fermentation-timing/)
3. Shape and refrigerate

Gather the dough gently and finish shaping with enough tension to hold the loaf. Place it in a prepared basket, cover and refrigerate according to the source method, which gives a 12–24 hour cold-proof window for this loaf. Note the actual start time and how strong the loaf felt before chilling. A different fridge or a much warmer dough can change how the loaf behaves the next day. [1](https://simmeringstarfruit.com/2026/02/22/whole-wheat-sourdough-bread/) [7](https://www.theperfectloaf.com/guides/proofing-bread-dough/)
4. Bake and cool

For the source’s Dutch-oven version, heat the oven to 450°F (about 232°C), using a vessel that permits the stated preheat. Score and bake covered for about 30 minutes, then uncover and finish for another 15–25 minutes. Check the source’s colour and internal doneness cues. Let the loaf cool on a rack before slicing through the centre. [1](https://simmeringstarfruit.com/2026/02/22/whole-wheat-sourdough-bread/) [8](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2023/05/31/how-to-tell-if-bread-is-done)

blocks.text: For a controlled comparison, use one formula at a time and record the variables that differ between this loaf and the white-flour beginner loaf. Those two published recipes use different starter proportions and methods, so the finished slices will reflect more than flour alone. To study flour specifically, use one method and run a single flour-blend change in a future bake. Record any water adjustment separately. [1](https://simmeringstarfruit.com/2026/02/22/whole-wheat-sourdough-bread/) [9](https://alexandracooks.com/2017/10/24/artisan-sourdough-made-simple-sourdough-bread-demystified-a-beginners-guide-to-sourdough-baking/) [2](https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2020/11/05/how-to-produce-an-open-crumb-in-sourdough-bread)

[Crispy Crust](/)’s planned formula and [bake journal](/journal/sourdough-bake-journal-template) would keep the exact flour blend, dough temperature and crumb photo together. That would make it easier to repeat a loaf before testing another bag of wholemeal flour or a small water change.
Decide what to repeat after the first loaf

Record the starter mix as well as the added flour. With the same added flour and a white 80% hydration starter, the whole wheat share would be 250 ÷ 600, about 41.7%. That example shows how two loaves called “50/50” can differ even before anyone changes the water. If the loaf was tight at shaping, compare dough temperature and bulk cues on a repeat before adjusting hydration. If it felt unusually loose from the first mix, start by checking weights and flour identity. Keep the oven and proof plan as comparable as possible so the next loaf gives you a clearer signal.
